Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 35 to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act. He said: There is one provision of this Bill which is of general application; its purpose is to raise the age at which persons defined as children may be committed to reformatories instead of to penitentiaries or goals. The present age limit is sixteen years; the Bill proposes to raise it to eighteen years. There have been pretty widespread representations on the desirability of this change. Furthermore its desirability has been impressed upon my mind from observation of cases of very young people, slightly over sixteen years of age, who have been committed to the penitentiaries, which, under the present law, was the only place to which they could be committed. The other provisions of the Bill are to meet proposed changes in the reformatory system in the province of Nova Scotia, in order to adjust our legislation to meet those changes which are desired by the provincial authorities. I think there will be an opportunity later on of fully explaining those proposed changes.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
AMES	[DOT]
On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE. KING (Leader of the Opposition) :	Mr. Speaker, in
view of the declaration of Sir Herbert Ames, which was communicated by you to the House yesterday, and which appears

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
duly recorded in the Journals of the House at page 104 of the Votes and Proceedings of March 17, I desire to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) for an explanation of the answers which have been made to certain questions asked in this House respecting the resignation of the former member for St. Antoine. The declaration to which I have referred is as follows:	.
To the Honourable Speaker of the House of Commons:
I, Herbert B. Ames, member for the House of Commons of Canada, for the electoral district of St. Antoine, Montreal, do hereby resign my seat in the said House of Commons, for the constituency aforesaid.
Given under my hand and seal at Ottawa, this fourteenth day of February, A.D. 1921.
Herbert B. Aimes. (L.S.)
Witness, W. S. Middlebro.
Witness, Howard P. Whiidden.
I would direct the attention of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister to the fact that it is set forth in this declaration that it was given under the hand and seal of Sir Herbert Ames at Ottawa on the 14th day of February, 1921. The 14th of February was the day of the opening of the present session of Parliament. I would also direct his attention to the fact that the witnesses to the declaration are the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) the chief whip of the Government party, and the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Whidden). It is known that Sir Herbert Ames has not been in Canada during the present year; he has been in Europe and has been there for some months.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to have to remind the hon. gentleman that while I wish to allow every latitude in the statement which he is making for the purpose of leading up to a question, it would be highly improper on his part to make any argument on the Orders of the Day when .here is no subject before the Chair. The hon. member, if he desired to go into the question fully, would have an opportunity to do so at any time on a motion to go into Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no desire to present an argument, but I regard it as material to an understanding of the significance of the questions which I am about to read that I should direct the attention of the House to the date to which I have just referred. The first question with reference to the resignation of Sir Herbert Ames was asked by the hon. mem-

ber for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) in the course of the debate on the Address. This question, which was asked on March 2 and will be found on page 489 of Hansard (unrevised), was as follows:
There is another matter to which I wish to direct your attention. Mr. Speaker. On July 21, 1920, the hon. member for Ste. Antoine. Montreal (Sir Herbert Ames), delivered a very eloquent address before the Empire Parliamentary Association in London on "The Dominions and the League of Nations.'' This address was printed, and I have a copy of it in my hand. With your permission, I will read the following words from page 5 :
"Now, I have just returned from a hurried visit to Canada. Mr. Balfour has alluded to the double capacity which I occupied at that time, and for the moment still occupy. For sixteen years I have been the representative of Western Montreal in the Canadian House of Commons. My resignation is in the hands of the Speaker because I have found thait my new work is quite enough to occupy all the time and attention that I am capable of giving to it."
This was on July 21, 1920. Why should the electors of St. Antoine, Montreal, be disfranchised? Why has the resignation of Sir Herbert Ames been kept secret and withheld? I am sure that it must have been intercepted on its way to Your Honour, because you could not have it in your hands without acting upon it-but that is always the humiliating method of avoiding an election and evading a defeat. Shall this be permitted to continue? Will the Canadian people stand for that much longer?
To this question, you, Mr. Speaker, made the following reply immediately upon eon-elusion of the speech of my hon. friend:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Two references in the
speech of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) make it highly essential, 1 think, that the position of the Chair should be stated clearly and beyond all question	
The second reference to which I wish to allude has to do with the statement credited to the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) that his resignation was in the Speaker's hands. The House will at once realize that it would never do for the impression to go abroad that the Speaker was a party to withholding a document of that character.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I therefore deem it my duty to make it clear to the House that I have not in my possession the resignation of the member for St. Antoine, nor have I ever received a document which was, or which purported to be, the resignation of his seat in this House.
On March 3, the day following, I addressed the following question on the Orders of the Day to the right hon. Prime Minister. It will be found on page 506 of Hansard:

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: THE MEMBER FOR ST. ANTOINE, MONTREAL

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: THE MEMBER FOR ST. ANTOINE, MONTREAL
speechtext:
Is the
Prime Minister aware, of the hon. mofriber

for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) having made any public declaration to the effect that he had tendered his resignation as a member of this Parliament? Has the Prime Minister or any other member of the Government received an intimation from that hon. gentleman of his desire or intention to tender his resignation?
To this question the right, hon. the Prime Minister replied:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE MEMBER FOR ST. ANTOINE, MONTREAL

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
1.	Is it true that the member for Saint Antoine, Montreal, has sent in his resignation as a member of the House of Commons?
2.	If so, when was it received by the Speaker of the House?
It was replied to as follows, by you, Mr. Speaker:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The answer to the first
question is, No. The second question is answered by the reply to No. 1.
In justice, Mr. Speaker, to Sir Herbert Ames himself and to hon.; members of this House, I should like to ask the Prime Minister how it comes that this document, bearing the signatures of hon. members opposite as witnesses, happens to be dated at Ottawa on the 14th of February, of the present year, when Sir Herbert Ames, so far as is known, was in Europe at that date and has been in Europe all of the present year? Assuming that the declaration was made on the date set forth, the second question I should like to ask my right hon. friend is, who is responsible for having withheld this important document from you, Mr. Speaker, for over a month, from February 14 until March 17? The third question is, in view of the existence of this declaration by Sir Herbert Ames, what explanation has the Prime Minister to make of the answers given to the questions I have just quoted?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Noting, as I have, the formality with which the leader of the Opposition has framed his questions and the rather long recitals which preceded them, I suggest that it would have been fairer had he given
me notice of the subject matter; but that has not been his practice. However, there will be no difficulty at all in replying to his questions. Every answer given in this House by the Government as read by my hon. friend is absolutely correct. I knew of no public declaration Sir Herbert Ames had made; if Sir Herbert Ames himself had stated-I had not seen the statement before 

that his resignation was at the time mentioned in the Speaker's hands, it could not have been correct. His resignation was not in the Speaker's hands until shortly before the time Mr. Speaker announced it. The fact is that Sir Herbert Ames had his resignation made out and left with a friend, to be dated within certain limits fixed by him. His instructions were fully carried out and the resignation forwarded accordingly.
TEMPERATURE OF THE CHAMBER On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to direct the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCurdy) to a matter which, while not of urgent public importance, is of some importance to the members of this House. I refer to the temperature of the Chamber. For a week or more the Chamber has on frequent occasions been extremely draughty and quite cold, and I would like to ask the Minister whether it is not possible for him to make such arrangements as will enable us to do business in ordinary comfort.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. B. McCURDY (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The complaint which has been made by the hon. member has come from various parts of the Chamber, and concurrently complaints have come from other members that the temperature is too high. The official in charge of heating has instructions to keep the temperature of the Chamber as near as possible to 67 degrees, which, I believe, is proper for a House of this character whether on the Government side or in the shades of Opposition.
INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION On the Orders of the Day:
Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Three
Rivers and St. Maurice) :	I see by an
Ottawa despatch in the Montreal Gazette that the Prime Minister has notified all parties interested in the Lake of the Woods control legislation to appear at Ottawa to present their case on Monday next at 11.30 o'clock. Have the parties representing the Americans and

the parties representing Canada on the International Joint Commission also been notified? I will put the question otherwise. Has the International Joint Commission been notified to appear with the Manitoba, Ontario, and other people interested?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is, on Monday at 11.30?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. Monday at 11.30 has been fixed as the date on which any parties interested in the legislation who wished to make representations against it may be heard by the Government. The International Joint Commission, neither American nor Canadian section, has, so far as any knowledge has reached us, any objection to this legislation.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I should like to call the attention of the Government to an article appearing in the Montreal Gazette this morning regarding the Roumanian bonds. The article reads:
Roumanian bonds pay no dividends. Canada's chances of securing interest soon are very slim. Canada's chances of securing payment of the irterest on the bonds representing the $25,000,000 loaned to the Roumanian Government two years ago as a trade credit has practically disappeared for the present.
The article further states:
The Roumanian Government now states that ir is unable to pay these bonds, and proposes that they be renewed for one year, offering to pay interest at the rate of 8 J per cent instead of the 5 per cent originally fixed.
Is the Government aware of these facts, and has any proposition been made to the Canadian Government regarding a settlement of bonds and interest?

My recollection is that this matter has already been dealt with by a formal question and answer already given to the House. It is not new. The interest has not been paid. The only thing Roumania is now suggesting is that we should agree to defer our claim for interest, so that that interest would not be in default.
Has the Government arrived at any decision?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government is endeavouring to collect the debt.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

There appears in this morning's papers an article relating to the resumption of trade between Great Britain and Russia. Is it the intention of the Canadian Government also to resume trade relations with Russia, and in that case, will the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) have his trade agents instructed to see what business openings are available for Canadian trade or will he leave Canadian interests to look after the trade themselves. I would point out to the right hon. gentleman that, owing to the difficulties of communication with Russia at present, it might be preferable that his trade agents be instructed to look out for business openings.
If my right hon. friend will kindly refer to Hansard of yesterday, he will find my answer to a question which is almost precisely the same as his.
May I ask the Minister of Finance if there is such a thing now as a Russian national currency?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that that is a question of which due notice ought to be given.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier):
speechtext: I see by the press that Mr. Lloyd George has declared that a commission is to investigate shortly the matter of the embargo on Canadian cattle. Has the Government any official knowledge of that and, if so, does it intend to be represented before or on that commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Government has received a communication from the High Commissioner to the effect that such a commission was promised by the British Prime Minister. The terms of the commission have not yet reached the Government. It will depend upon the terms of the commission what action we should take, but I would think, undoubtedly, the Government would see to it that the facts in support of Canada's contention will be fully and carefully laid before that commission.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: Has the Prime Minister observed a despatch stating that the Prime Minister of Australia intends to acquaint the Australian Parliament with the subjects to be taken up at the approaching conference in London and to give that Parliament an opportunity of discussing them? Is it my right hon. friend's intention to give this Parliament the same statement and a like opportunity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had not observed any statement by the Australian Prime Minister to the effect described by the hon. gentleman, but I had myself moved in the matter and a little earlier than he. I have already given this House, in outline, the subjects that will probably be discussed. The exact agenda has not yet reached us, but the three important topics that had been suggested were stated in an answer made about three weeks ago to the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault) and the answer to his question went on to state that, should it appear the desire of a substantial number of members that special opportunity be afforded in this House for discussion, it would be provided. Ever since that, at any time on occasions when subjects such as that might be brought up, the subject might have been discussed. Should further information reach us making certain that other important topics would be considered, I will feel it my duty to state those topics or their substance to the House.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item No. 4 Justice

salaries-contingencies-
The consent of the House is necessary before this item is called, because the Estimates of this particular department have not been taken up before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We had understood-
I hope, not misunderstood-that we would be permitted to go into Justice. Might I remind the hon. gentleman that I did not absolutely insist on my rights the other evening and, perhaps, one good turn deserves another.

I claim that a minister
who wants to go on with his Estimates like this, should, before going on, ask for the consent of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite concede that.
If I was under a misapprehension, I am sorry, but I thought the House understood that I was to go on.
It was announced definitely last night that agriculture would be taken up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And Justice.

The Prime Minister
said any others might be taken up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said Justice as well.
Members of the House must consent to that. The announcement of my right hon. friend is not sufficient.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I quite agree with that, but let me read what I said last night:
Mr. Fielding: What business will be taken up to-morrow?
Mr. Meighen: The motion to go into Supply.
Mr. Fielding: On the same Estimates?
Mr. Meighen: On the same Estimates and those of the Department of Justice, and any others that we may have a right to go on with.
Mr. Bureau: That is rather vague.
Mr. Meighen: I do not think that there are any others that we have a right to go on with, consequently they could not be taken up but by consent. If we do ask for consent it will be on the Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. If all those go through, we will proceed with Government orders.
So the Department of Justice was specially mentioned, it being the understanding, as I was informed by my hon. friend, that he would be permitted to go on, in view of the fact that he did not insist on his right to go on with his Estimates on Tuesday night, I think it was, when they were reached.

My object is not to raise any opposition, but to affirm a right. I do not think this vote should be called by the chairman before a formal motion is made asking for the unanimous consent of the House. There is no objection to giving unanimous consent, but it ought to go on the record that that is the proper procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I quite recognize that I am not entitled to proceed without the consent of the House, and I beg through the chairman to ask whether the House is prepared to consent to my taking up the items I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point raised by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is, of course, as admitted by the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) well taken. The Estimates of the Department of Justice having not yet been

taken up this session, and this being Friday, it is necessary that the committee should give its unanimous consent before these Estimates can be considered. Is it the unanimous desire of the committee that the Estimates of the Department of Justice be now considered?
Carried.
If the objection of one member is sufficient to prevent the Justice Estimates being proceeded with now, I wish to object.

May I ask my right hon. friend what is the difficulty about proceeding with the Agriculture Estimates? We were in the midst of a very interesting discussion last night, and we do not want to lose the thread of our thoughts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no objection at all to proceeding with Agriculture first, but I understood from the Minister of Agriculture last night that there were only four items left, and we thought it would likely expedite matters if we went on with the Justice Estimates first, and took up the four remaining items in the Agriculture Estimates later. I think the long experience of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's will lead him to concur with me in that expectation.
I do not want to call attention to the fact that the Government might have insisted on its right to go into the Justice Estimates the other night, especially as it promised that ample opportunity would be given for a motion on going into Supply on another day on the Justice Estimates. That having been done, I think it is hardly fair that objection should be raised. However, it has been raised, and we will go on with the Department of Agriculture.
Department of Agriculture-Publications, $34,500.
Would the minister explain what these publications are?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Our Publications Branch was located at 66 Queen Street, but we are now moving to the Robinson Building on the same street. We publish what is known as the Agricultural Gazette. It is published about six times a year, and has in its columns all the latest information regarding agriculture. It is distributed to the Departments of Agriculture in the various provinces, institutions of learning, agricultural societies, and members of Parliament. The Publications Branch also maintains a distribution office, through which the reports and bulletins of the department
[The Chairman.]
are issued. During the last five years this branch has distributed some 13,000,000 bulletins and during seven months of the present year 1,150,000. The branch also prepares press notices.

Are these publications intended to be distributed to the agricultural societies in the different provinces? If that is not already being done, I think it would be a very good idea, because while these societies may get instructions from other sources, direct instruction from the Minister of Agriculture by means of these reports would be of great assistance to the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to the Agricultural Gazette?
Yes, and other publications of the Branch.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The general course
followed is to distribute the publications to those who directly apply for them. We have found that if distributed freely, the publications often fall into the hands of men who have no particular interest in them, do not read them, and consequently do not benefit. But when a man takes the trouble to write a letter for a certain publication, we assume that he takes an interest in the work in question, and the publication is sent with some beneficial object in view. We do not distribute except to people who send in an application, but we gladly send our publications to those who do.

I would suggest that the
different publications be sent either to the Governments of the different provinces, or to the secretaries of the agricultural societies in each province. In New Brunswick we have about eight or ten agricultural societies. I think this would afford a direct channel of instruction to the farmers throughout the country, and would prove very valuable.

Does the
minister think that the nation gets full value from the expenditure on the Agricultural Gazette and these various leaflets? This item is not a very large one, and I have no desire to obstruct, I need not tell my hon. friend, but we all realize the need of economy, and it has got to be begun somewhere. There is nothing I am more struck with in connection with government generally than the deluge of printed matter that descends upon the heads of members of Parliament and, I assume, upon the Senators also. It would be a mistake for me to judge the activities

of my fellow-members by my own, so I will content myself with saying that I have not time to read anything like all the material that is sent to me, not only from this department but from other departments of the Government. If I did, I should have no time for the Scriptures, and that would be a very serious matter for me, as for other hon. members. I see my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) smiles, but it is not quite a smiling matter, I may tell him. Is the minister quite sure that we get value in these publications? Thirteen millions of leaflets is a tremendous crop.
I am not sure that all the crops raised under the Department of Agriculture bear anything like a fair relationship to this one. But I am confident that if this particular crop is meant for seed, then more of this seed goes to waste in the ground than most of the other crops raised under the direction of my genial and able friend.

Perhaps the minister will allow me to ask a question before he replies to my hon. friend. Is there any systematic scheme of circulating these blue books that are printed in the department? From my own knowledge the information contained in some of these publications is valuable and so long as money is expended in printing them, and the postage is free, I think it is unfortunate that this literature shodld not find its way to the farmers. I am sure it would do them some good. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), says that his whole time is occupied in reading the Scriptures. Well, if he does not gain any better results from his reading of the blue books than he does from his perusal of Holy Writ, I would say let us publish no more blue books. However, that is a mere aside. When the money in connection with this work is spent and the pamphlets are published, it is really too bad that they should be thrown away from year to year. But it is evident that they must be discarded if they are not sent to the farmers, and a little extra labour would put them into circulation so that the people generally, and particularly the farmers, would be able to get the benefit of the information thus published. Let me urge upon the minister the necessity for the widest possible circulation of all literature prepared by his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
First of all, for the information of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), I think that excellent results are obtained from the distribution of these bulletins. We do not distribute them except to those who send in their
names with a request to be placed on our mailing list. Those who desire to have these publications select bulletins dealing with the particular line of work in which they are interested, and the mere fact that they go to the trouble of writing to the department and requesting that they be supplied with these publications, is abundant evidence that they are interested and are anxious to have information. As a pratical farmer and stock man I have derived a great deal of benefit, not only from our Canadian bulletins, but from United States publications. For a number of years I kept my name on the mailing list at Washington for agricultural bulletins, and I can assure the committee that on various occasions the information contained in a single publication, if followed, was enough to ensure success, while ignorance of the instruction imparted would, in all probability, mean failure. Now, let me make it clear that we carefully watch the situation in order to prevent any waste in these pamphlets, and the plan of sending publications only to those who request them has worked out as economically as any scheme could.
How much per year is spent on the Agricultural Gazette?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The expenditure for this year is $18,000.

Will the minister be kind enough to see that copies of all his publications are distributed throughout the county of Kamouraska? I had occasion to refer to this matter the other day. The agricultural school at St. Anne de la Pocatiere, as I was informed by the professor a few days ago in a letter which I sent to the King's Printer, has not been receiving all the bulletins published by the department. The same thing applies to the classical college in the same place. The greater part of that institution	was
destroyed by fire last winter, and the library containing over 35,000 volumes was completely wiped out. I wish the Minister would note these facts and see that these institutions are properly supplied. I might add that the school of domestic science for girls at St. Pascal is also in need of such publications of the department as are suitable for the work there. I am sure the minister recognizes the needs of these schools. As I said the other day, his deputy frequently visits the county of Kamouraska and is aware of its importance, and I think he will agree with me that the requests of these colleges for these publications are only reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Both these institutions are now on the mailing list, but if they are not receiving a sufficient number of copies of any publication, or, as the hon. member suggests, are not receiving some publications at all, I shall be only too glad to look into the matter and see to it that they are both properly supplied.
The minister is evidently overlooking the third. May I remind him of the school for girls at St. Pascal?

I have seen in the press the statement that the department has decided to discontinue the' publication of the Gazette, the explanation being that the ground is so well covered by agricultural magazines throughout the country that there is no great necessity for this particular publication. I have in my hand another publication issued by the department, and one which has been very freely distributed throughout the western part of Ontario in all public places such as banks and post offices, where there is a fine stack piled up on desks for people to make use of. There is on the cover of this publication a map showing the location of the various farms, and the following inscription accompanies the picture:
In the above map, note the location of experimental farms and stations. The superintendent of the experimental farm or station nearest to you will be pleased to give you any information in his power. Why not communicate Vvitn him ?
Well, it is rather unfortunate, as one may discover from a study of this map, that the experimental farms are practically all in Eastern and Western Canada. It is true that about five hundred miles west of here there is a little tobacco farm in the county of Essex, I think, or Kent. But many of the people throughout Western Ontario are not very much interested in the growing of tobacco. I would suggest that if it is not the intention to provide experimental farms in western Ontario, then this circular should be distributed where it is more acceptable, because it is an absolute waste of money to publish this pamphlet and leave it in public places in that part of the country for distribution when there is not one person out of a thousand in Western Ontario who is greatly concerned about the growing of tobacco, and that is the only farm with which people could communicate. More than that, this circular has, in the past, been very largely circulated in the Old Country, having been available there in the emigration offices, and I want to point out 
that it conveys a very unfair impression to the prospective immigrant regarding this country. He looks over this map and sees the location of these farms, and finds that Ontario is scarcely recognizable on the map. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not in a position
to say what would be a fair and equitable salary for the deputy minister of agriculture, or the deputy minister of another department; but parliament in 1913 or 1914, fixed the salary for the deputy minister of justice at $10,000 and it has continued at that figure ever since. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are all working

It is the work of Griffenhagen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The designations to
which the hon. gentleman refers are the result of the classification as applied to existing officers. I do not think we have
made one addition to the number this year, in fact the estimates show that 4 p.m. to be the case. Are they appointed by

Their salaries were

Will the minister say which of these officers appoints the lawyers who represent the department before the different courts in the respective judicial districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that as a rule the lawyers are selected because of the nature of the different cases. It is not a matter of practice to appoint a lawyer to do all the business in a district. In many instances it does happen there is one lawyer who deals with practically all the cases; but as I understand the practice, lawyers are selected rather with a view to particular cases and the particular business to be done. That selection is usually done by the assistant deputy minister in consultation with the deputy minister, and occasionally with the minister.

The reason I ask the

In these days when there is "no political patronage" I would like to know what officer it is who knows the lawyers so well as to always select the few Conservative lawyers, in the city of Quebec for instance, when there is a case in which the Department of Justice is interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall make enquiry
as to who has that particular scent.

It is a matter of
intuition.

It must be a
matter of instinct.

I understand there are law officers in every department of the Government. Do these officers relieve the counsel of the Justice Department of any of their work, or do the latter take up en banc the various questions that are submitted to their department after the law officers have passed on them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Everything is subject to review by the Department of Justice as provided in the statutes. When matters call for litigation, or serious questions arise, they are always submitted to the Department of Justice. I understand that these law clerks-I think it is rather a misnomer-are in the different departments for the convenience of being available with .regard to purely routine matters that require to be dealt with from day to day.

When the Crown is represented in the courts by the officers of the Department of Justice-the deputy minister or some of these counsel,-and costs are allowed to the. Crown, who gets those costs, the department or the counsel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Crown gets the costs-when they are paid.
It seems to me that when a lawyer acting for the Crown is successful and gets costs, surely that should be enough to encourage him to do as well the next time or better.
Every lawyer does the best he can at all times.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That argument is of general application, but we are fortunate in having lawyers who do so well that they need no encouragement to do better.

speechtext: I do not know that the duties can be described as being much heavier, t was the law though, and this lady-I am sure that will appeal to the hon. gentleman-gradually acquired this large salary by reason of the additional number of years she has been in the service; and I suppose, from a lady's point of view it is worth a good deal to have to admit the acquisition of those additional years. I do not suppose that, like the laws of the Medes and Persians, this system cannot be changed. It seems to be very unfair.

No, the position is

I see in the Estimates "Allowances to Private Secretaries." Has the minister two private secretaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; and I am blessed in the fact that they are both bi-lingual. One is a gentleman whose mother tongue is English and the other is a gentleman whose mother tongue is French. We have a very considerable French correspondence in the department, and I do not think we would be able to get along with less assistance in that regard.

Does not the

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I always seek to set
the kind of example that ought to be followed.
What salaries are being paid to these private secretaries?

One gets $3,360 and
the other $3,180.

Does that include $600

No, that is the salary

The allowances to private

The other $600 is for
the secretary of the Solicitor General.

I have never been able to
understand why these allowances are made to private secretaries in addition to their salaries. Why should not their salaries be inclusive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is a survival of
an old practice also, and it applies to all private secretaries appointed under that system.
I know it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the old practice, when a private secretary was appointed he became a clerk in the department with the salary attached to whatever class he was assigned to, and this $600 allowance was made because of the fact, as I understand it, that the private secretary of the minister-differing in that respect from other clerks-is not called upon to attend simply during the fixed hours of the day; he has to be at the disposal of the minister late and early when the minister needs him.

Late possibly rather than
early.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In some instances more often late than early. But it may be a little more burdensome on some persons to be late. I understand that is the reason
why that special allowance was fixed. With regard to those to whom it still applies, they are gentlemen who were in that position when that was settled, and to take it away from them now would be equivalent to reducing their salaries.

I have no desire to suggest

What is the name of the purchasing agent of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Dillon.
Is that gentleman still in business as a druggist?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not that I have any knowledge of.
Is it not the rule that the purchasing agent of a department must not engage in any outside business; that he must give his whole time and attention to the work of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Can the minister say that Mr. Dillon is not engaged in the business of selling drugs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no knowledge of his being engaged in that business. Shortly before the session opened, the members of Parliament received a circular letter from a gentleman who described himself, if I mistake not, as the head of a purchasing commission, which had been formed in direct contradiction to the will of Parliament. The matter was brought up last session and the session before and an attempt made to form a purchasing commission, but the measure was not carried because hon. gentlemen on both sides were opposed to it. Shortly before the session

opened a commission was formed by Order in Council. This being the case, why should there be any purchasing agents for the different departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite mistaken when he suggests that a purchasing commission was appointed in direct opposition to the decision of Parliament. He is quite mistaken, and so is the hon. gentleman who shakes his head, because I do not think either of them know the nature of the commission that was appointed under Order in Council. It was a totally different thing from what was contemplated by statute; it made provision for general supervision and direction, by one body, of the purchasing of the different departments. Even when we had a purchasing commission with the wider powers, appointed under the War Measures Act, that commission acted in direct communication with the purchasing agents of the different departments, who submitted to the Purchasing Commission their operations. When the supervisory or directing commission to which the hon. gentleman refers was appointed, the same system continued as between them and the purchasing agents of the different departments.

purchasing agent for the Department of Justice before the War Purchasing Commission was instituted?

What is comprised in the item "miscellaneous expenditure"?

Why is there a living allowance for the judge of Atlin district, B.C.?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was provided for at the time of his appointment. We went into the question a year or two ago whether the conditions still justified the payment of this living allowance, and we satisfied ourselves that they did. It is further to be said that the gentleman accepted the appointment with that provision made at the time. Quite apart from that, however, the district is a remote one and I think that the conditions fully justify the granting of a living allowance.
Is the cost of living any higher there than elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
give the details just now. As I stated, we went into the question a couple of years ago, and we felt satisfied that it was preferable to continue the allowance. It must further, of course, be considered whether it would be right, years after the gentleman had accepted the appointment with this allowance attached to it, for us to intervene now to take it away. Such action

1U81
might, perhaps, be open to question. In any new cases, we have avoided providing such allowances, and with the exception of the Yukon where an allowance is provided by law, this is the only case of the kind.

As questions concerning judges are now in order, I should like to ask an explanation regarding what appears to be a conflict of opinion, or a misunderstanding, with regard to the number of judges in the judicial district of Quebec. Last year, according to the new law concerning the organization of tribunals in that province, the number of King's Bench judges was increased. As my right hon. friend will remember, the judge who was sitting for the district of Beauce (Mr. Justice Flynn) was appointed to the King's Bench court, and the district of Beauce has been deprived of a judge for over a year until recently a new judge, I think (Mr. Justice D'Auteuil), was appointed for that district. What happens is this. One of the judges of the judicial district of Qtfebec, Mr. Justice Cannon, died some time ago, and the vacancy has not been filled. Is it the intention of the minister to appoint a judge to replace Mr. Justice Cannon, or is it true that this vacancy will not be filled? There is a misunderstanding about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not the present
intention to make a nomination to fill the vancancy to which the hon. member refers. In the first place, the delay in regard to the district of Beauce in particular, was, I think, attributable to the fact that a modification of the provincial law is in contemplation so as to do away with the attachment of judges to particular districts. At one time, it was anticipated that that modification would go through more promptly than has proved to be the case. When it became evident that there was to be a delay, we filled the position in the district of Beauce. I think there was a misunderstanding about an additional judge in the district of Quebec. At the time that the system in the province was changed, whereby the number of judges in the court of appeals was largely increased and the number of judges in the superior court was decreased, legislation of the province was so enacted as to call for a new additional judge. At the time I felt very strongly in regard tp the matter, and I called the attention of the Attorney General of the province to the fact that, when there were being made in the constitution of the courts in our
province, changes involving such a large' additional burden upon the Dominion treasury, it seemed to me to be not an occasion for increasing the number of judges, but, on the contrary, an occasion on which an effort ought to be made to avoid such increases as that. I may say that I believed the strongest justification for a change in the system was that it ought to conduce to making a lesser number of judges necessary. I am not suggesting that there should be a reduction from the old number, but the change ought to conduce to avoiding the necessity of an increase in the number. At the time that legislation was under discussion between us, I clearly pointed out that I thought there should not be an increase at that time, and in the legislation which I proposed should be enacted in this House, I did not contemplate making provision for both the numerous increases that were involved in salaries and a further increase in the number of judges. It is true that, if we read our statute as we passed it last year, there is room under it for an additional judge. That was the result of an error, pure and simple and this is how it came about. Under our previous statute there were enumerated a certain number of judges for the district of Montreal and a certain number for the district of Quebec, and the section went on to say that when the Chief Justice was in the other district, one of the fixed number would be the acting Chief Justice. In drawing up the new statute provision was made in a separate section for the acting Chief Justice, and then precisely the same number of judges was repeated when it came to deal with the puisne judges, it being overlooked that we had taken one of those and provided for him under the title of acting Chief Justice; so that when I went oyer the number for the purpose of satisfying myself that we were not increasing the number, I found that, owing to the fact that I have just mentioned, we did not apparently in words at all events, increase the number. I think our friends in Quebec ought to realize- and I trust there is a disposition to do so- that they should not press at the present time for an increase in the number of judges. Let the new system have a trial, and let us see whether it will produce, what I think we all agree in hoping it will produce, namely, results which will make it possible to carry on with a smaller number of judges. One would think the concentration ought to produce that result. For these reasons, I did not have in contemplation



making a nomination for that additional judgeship at the present time.

The net result is that there is one judge less for the judicial district of Quebec, and legal business is suffering very much on that account. There is, at the present time, an accumulation of cases, and all the lawyers and, of course, their litigants are complaining about the matter. If there is no change such as my right hon. friend suggests, namely, that all the judges should reside in Quebec and administer justice there, and tour the district, I do not see what the remedy will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am assured by the Premier of the province, who has transmitted to us a Bill for that purpose, that he intends to put the Bill through this session. I do not, however, want to tie that hon. gentleman down, because something may happen. And I cannot control the matter. Moreover, I rather understood that any immediate overcrowding that there was, was in large measure due to the unfortunate fact that certain of the judges were not in good health and, therefore, not able to carry on their work at the moment. I think the hon. gentleman will realise that the remedy for a momentary condition like that is not by increasing the number of judges, because we hope these gentlemen will recover their health, or in case they should not recover, they will be replaced by gentlemen capable of carrying on the work. I have every hope there will be goodwill enough in the province, in which I have confidence, and in that particular district of it, at all events, to give us a fair opportunity to try out the system and see whether we cannot carry on without an increase in the number of judges.
What is the limit of leave given to a judge who is in poor health and who is not able to fulfil his duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The law makes no absolute provision as to what leave you can give. Of course when a judge is so ill as not to be able to go to court and do his work, it does not make very much difference whether you give him leave or not, because if he is in a condition where he cannot do the work, the work will not be done because you refuse to give him leave. Last year-and I am pleased to mention this, and I should like hon. gentlemen to think it over-I did give notice of a resolution looking to a petition for such modification of the British North America Act as might make it possible for the Government in instanced where a judge's usefulness had

entirely ceased, without its being a question of misbehaviour on his part, to have the facts established and to have the judge removed. I gave notice of that resolution, but did not proceed with it because I was given to understand there would be very strenuous opposition to it and I did not desire to propose a resolution looking to an amendment of our Constitution unless there would be substantial agreement upon it among the members of this Parliament. I take this opportunity of mentioning it again, and I would be glad if hon. gentlemen would give a little thought to the matter, and see if they cannot alter their attitude, in which event I should be glad to re-introduce the resolution.
There is a very serious difficulty that arises under the present provision of the British North America Act. A judge is appointed for life-he is appointed, rather, during good behaviour. I think that is an excellent provision so far as it goes. It, of course, makes the judge absolutely independent; he is quite beyond any governmental control, and I think that in principle that is quite right. The only method by which, even if you charge him with misbehaviour, any action can be taken looking to terminating his holding of office is by an impeachment before both Houses of Parliament, and every one will realize that that is a very cumbersome mode of procedure, even if it be applicable in all cases.
Then there is this other consideration. The judge is appointed, as I have said, during good behaviour. Now it is perhaps susceptible of suggestion, perhaps' more than suggestion, that the mere fact that a judge has ceased to be physically able to do his work is not a case of bad behaviour-though I may say, speaking for myself, personally I would be disposed to believe that where a judge has become incapable of doing his work, it can hardly be described as good behaviour-for him to insist on holding his office and refrain from resigning. Now we have in different parts of the country some cases, at all events, where I think that is fairly the situation, and it was to enable us to deal with such cases that I made the suggestion last year.

I approve the minister's suggestion. I do not think any distinction should be made between Supreme Court and County Court judges in the matter of incapacity to perform their duties. If a County Court judge is not capable of performing his duties, and does not want to ask for superannuation, the Government can force him to retire. I do not see why

that should not apply also to Superior Court judges. There are some judges who have not performed their duties for many months, and perhaps have no prospect of performing them in the future, but they do not want to ask for superannuation because they are drawing a higher salary than they would receive if retired. But the interests of the litigants suffer, and I think it is only proper that the Government should be given power to force those judges to ask for superannuation.

With regard to the
reorganization in the province of Quebec, I have already drawn * the attention of the Minister of Justice to how it is working in a part of the province, especially the district of Hull. I think the reorganization has not proved a great success, especially in that part of the province. In principle, centralization was good for the larger centres. It gave them the advantage of having a greater number of judges, but in the rural districts, especially those that are remote, such as the district of Hull, the result has been to deprive them of the judges who were administering justice. I drew the minister's attention to that state of affairs lest sesion. Since the new law has been in operation, I have no complaint to make of the Chief Justice in Montreal, but our district has not had the advantage of having the requisite number of judges to administer justice. Under the reorganization, Quebec and Montreal have been considered the two main centres of the province, but there are also two other centres of some importance, Three Rivers and Sherbrooke. I think the city of Hull should have been included with these two, on account of its importance. In the matter of population it is larger than either Three Rivers or Sherbrooke, and for these reasons and in view also of its remoteness from Montreal, I think it should have been included with these other two cities. Whether it is on account of the small number of judges, or because we are a considerable distance from Montreal, the fact remains that we did not have a judge to attend to our term. We used to have one residing judge, and a second judge administering justice in Hull, and we used to have twenty or twenty-one days of term every month. It was necessary for the expeditious despatch of business that two judges should administer justice there, but since the new law has been in operation, we have not had five days of term every month for the administration of justice. We have, however, sometimes had the advantage of a
69J
judge from Montreal, and we appreciate that very much. I think it is my duty to call the minister's attention to this state of affairs, and I hope he will confer, if necessary, with the Chief Justice in Montreal, or with the Attorney General of the province, in order that the necessary number of judges for the administration of justice may be appointed, and also in order that this reorganization may be amended in order to have the city of Hull placed on the same footing as Three Rivers and Sherbrooke, so that we will have the privilege of residing judges in the future, as we had in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
doubtless appreciates that I am quite powerless with regard to determining how the districts shall be divided, or where the judges shall reside. That is a matter absolutely for the provincial authority to determine. As for conferring with the Chief Justice, or with the Attorney General or Prime Minister of the province, I certainly will always be most happy to do so whenever they may think that my advice or a conference would be of service, but the hon. gentleman can understand that I have no quality to go forward and force any opinions of mine upon either of these gentlemen, whose duties are perfectly clearly defined. However, if I should be consulted on the matter, I shall be glad to bring to their attention what the hon. gentleman has represented with regard to conditions in his own particular district.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Exchequer Court, Canada, $8,333.34.
In this court, I understand, we have two judges, and if I remember rightly, provision was made a couple of years ago to appoint a third. Does the Government intend to make that appointment shortly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The matter is not in contemplation at present, although I should not like to speak positively. My impression is that the provision for the third judge was repealed. I may be wrong, but I had that idea. At present there is a president of the court and one judge. We have had no representations recently of there being any pressing need for a third judge, and the matter was therefore not in immediate contemplation.
I remember distinctly that provision was made for a third, and it never occurred to me that it had been repealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will send for the Judges' Act of last session. I am rather of the opinion that that Act made no provision for more than one judge in addition to the president of the court.
Whilst the Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court is acting on the Grand Trunk arbitration, is there a judge ad hoc?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No judge ad hoc has been appointed. We have not had any representation upon the subject, but in the statute there is a provision for such appointment if necessary upon representation.

Is it the intention of the Government also to appoint a judge in Vice Admiralty in the district of Quebec in the near future? I may point out that last year there were several cases pending before the Exchequer Court in Admiralty district, in the district of Quebec, and we were long delayed in the hearing of them because we had to wait until a judge in Vice Admiralty bf the district of Montreal, who is at the same time a judge of the Superior Court bf that district, could come down to the city of Quebec, a thing which I think could easily be avoided if, as heretofore, a special judge were appointed. Since the death of Sir Basil Routhier, no judge has been appointed in the Vice Admiralty district of Quebec. Does the minister intend to appoint one in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot at the present time announce a decided view upon that subject. We have in the past appointed a judge of the Superior Court or, in some cases, a judge of the Court of King's Bench, to act as Vice Admiralty judge. There was one such judge in Montreal and one in Quebec. It has been suggested from respectable quarters, and there seems to be a good deal to say for the proposal, that there is no special reason why we should pick out a particular judge to discharge these duties. It has been said that the business might be more expeditiously disposed of if we left it as a matter in which all the judges of the court should have jurisdiction, without appointing a special Vice Admiralty judge. Of course, there has to be a Vice Admiralty court. As I say, I am not prepared to announce any final decision on the subject, but it has been under consideration, and we should come to a conclusion shortly. There would then arise the question, even if we decided to maintain the appointment of a distinct 
judge, whether there is really business to call for two judges in Vice Admiralty, in the province of Quebec. However, the matter will have careful attention.

I would suggest that a
judge in Vice Admiralty be appointed instead of giving jurisdiction to a number * of judges. Cases in Vice Admiralty, though numerous in the course of a year, are not so numerous as ordinary cases, and jurisprudence in Vice Admiralty cases is also quite different from ordinary civil jurisprudence. Now, if a judge were specially appointed, he would be better qualified to administer justice in Vice Admiralty cases than would be an ordinary judge of the civil court, no matter how devoted the latter might be to the performance of his duties. In this respect I think we were very fortunate in the past, as much in Montreal as in Quebec, in having judges well posted on precedence as well as on general jurisprudence in Admiralty cases; and I venture the suggestion that for the proper administration of justice it would be preferable to appoint a judge to have special jurisdiction in these cases. Such a man would be more familiar with the jurisprudence and law on these subjects than a judge who did not specialize in this direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is certainly
force in the suggestion.
The Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court hes been acting as a member of the Grand Trunk arbitration board for some months. Is he paid a salary or does he get fees for acting as arbitrator?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a provision
in the statute for remuneration to be paid by both parties to this particular arbitration. I do not think that the amount of the remuneration has been fixed.

I would suggest to the
minister to allow the judges in the different judical districts in the province of Quebec to act as judges under the Bankruptcy Act. In the judical district of Kamouraska, we have had a few assignments already under that new law, and we have encountered great difficulty and inconvenience by reason of the fact that we have no local judge. We have to apply to the judge in Montreal, and I think that the judge appointed under the Bankruptcy Act in Montreal will find enough to occupy him in the district of Montreal alone. All local judges should be appointed as judges under the Bankruptcy Act.

I oppose that contention
of my hon. friend.

You want them all in
Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is well I did not
speak before I discovered where you stand.

As I understand the Act, the object of appointing one judge for each province was to obtain uniformity in the new law respecting bankruptcy. Under the Bankruptcy Act, the judge can delegate certain powers he has to the local judge from time to time. Bue when it comes to dealing with large and important questions under the Bankruptcy law, it is well to have one judge in order that there might be no difference of opinion between the local judge and himself. Judges differ in the same way as lawyers, and if we had twenty-five or thirty superior judges, dealing with bankruptcy, the effect of the law would be rendered nugatory before we get very far. I think my hon. friend knows that under the Act the registrar has certain considerable powers; and when necessary, the Bankruptcy judge visits these districts from time to time to apply the law. I am opposed to the view of my hon. friend.

I think the contention of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Stein) is a very good one. If the argument advanced by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) were to prevail, the minister should appoint one judge for the whole of our province. Then we would have uniformity.

Civil and criminal cases
are just as important as commercial litigation. Criminal cases require celerty of treatment; that is why we require a local judge in each district. In one case that is pending I submitted some objections that I had to our registrar who argued that he was not authorized to allow them. We wrote to the judge and he would not then had to our registrar, who argued that he express any definite opinion. We had no time to wait until that judge came to the district, and our local judge had no authority to act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not sure that
this is a matter that rests with the Minister of Justice to deal with. If my.recollection of the Bankruptcy Act is correct, the Minister of Justice is empowered to appoint a judge on bankruptcy for each bankruptcy district so to speak. Now I believe each province is a bankruptcy district. I am of opinion, however, that power is vested
in the Secretary of State to divide a province into districts and create a larger number. That would be a preliminary condition before the Minister of Justice could take action in the matter. My own understanding of the Bankruptcy Act, and I speak with deference in the presence of the hon. member for George. Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) is, that through the powers which the judge in bankruptcy can confer upon his colleagues there is ample provision to meet the immediate wants of a particular district. In that, however, I may be mistaken. Of course, there is this further fact to be pointed out: If the provincial legislation to which I referred a little while ago should be carried out you would not in that event have in each district a resident judge even if you made him a bankruptcy judge. It had occurred to me, however, that if that legislation were carried out it might be a proper thing in the province of Quebec to create four bankruptcy districts, and in the province and there would then be four districts where there would be a resident judge. However that is not my function to determine, it is the duty of the Secretary of State. I shall be glad to confer with him on the subject, see what his view is, and try to establish a balance between the conflicting views of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and my hon. friends from Kamouraska (Mr. Stein) and Dorchester (Mr. Cannon).

Should not these districts
harmonize with the judicial districts which now exist? It seems to me that
5 p.m. there should he no distinction, and in that event the judges in each district could act under full authority with respect to the Bankruptcy Act as they do under any other Act. Further, in answer to the objection which the minister finds in the fact that the judges now residing in four main places of the province I would say this: These judges attend to the administration of justice in their districts at least once a month, so that there would be very litle delay if they were empowered to deal with these other matters-when they came to administer justice generally they could dispose of the other litigation as well.
I think the ends of justice would be better met if they were empowered to act in these other cases, and if the districts created under the Bankruptcy Act were made to t harmonize with the judicial districts generally. There is another question I would like to bring to the minister's attention. Under this item we are voting the salary of

the Marshal in Admiralty in the district of Quebec. Under what title does it fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed the
registrar is paid by fees. I know that was the practice when I had occasion to deal with the court in Montreal and I should suppose that the same practice prevails now.

We have in Quebec a ViceAdmiralty district. The district is organized, but unfortunately the registrar is obliged to provide all the stationery,-books, pens, ink and other material-and he receives a meagre pittance as far as fees are concerned. We are very fortunate in having a Mr. Bradley, the present registrar, a most competent man, and I think this faithful servant of the state should receive a little better consideration from the Government. I would urge the Government to grant this gentleman a salary, and also to provide him with all the necessary stationery and other supplies which are absolutely essential for the decent upkeep of the office in Quebec. This gentleman is very competent, well posted in the law, very faithful in the discharge of his duties, and should receive better treatment. I would urge the minister to give him a fixed salary, as the fees are so uncertain and vary so much from year to year that it will be impossible when this gentleman, who is over seventy years of age, passes away-[DOT] at least it will be very difficult-to find a successor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will be glad to look into the circumstances. Of course the hon. gentleman will see at a glance that if the business is so small that the fees do not provide a living for the registrar, it makes it a serious question whether we should maintain two separate admiralty courts in the province instead of having only one where the business would be sufficient with the fixed fees, to adequately remunerate the registrar. However, I shall look into the matter. It is not the first time I have heard of Mr. Bradley's good qualities and I shall give the subject sympathetic consideration.

As to the volume of business done I may point out to the minister that although in some years the amount is small, in other years it is really very considerable so that the court cannot be abolished. It would be a great inconvenience for those who are subject to Admiralty law in the district of Quebec if the court there were abolished. I would rather recommend to the Minister that he should

change the present system; that he should make the fees payable to the Government and pay a fixed salary to the registrar so as to ensure to the department the services of a good man.

I was not in the Chamber when my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) first spoke, but from what I have gathered he has been protesting to the Minister of Justice because no judge in Admiralty has been named in Quebec since the death of the late Judge Routhier. Now it is very inconvenient for pleaders in Quebec, and for the shipping concerns in that city and district, to be obliged to go to Montreal and pay the extra fee which they have to incur by reason of the transfer of cases to that city.
I understand that the bar of Quebec have protested against this and have asked the Minister of Justice to name some judge to replace the late Judge Routhier. I understand that it is possible for the Minister of Justice to nominate a practicing barrister to this position; and there is no real reason why he should not do it. I might say that the leader of the bar in admiralty practice in that province has had considerable experience, and, besides his professional qualifications, is eminently qualified from the standpoint of the minister-he has been a stern unbending Tory for many years, and as one of the pillars of the party in Quebec he has supported his party in its darkest days. Therefore it seems to me that there should be a certain amount of gratitude, even in Tory breasts, and that the minister ought to reward men of that type who have served their party so well and faithfully in the past. I hold no brief for Mr. Pentland. His qualifications are well known to the bar and to the shipping interests of the city of Quebec, and they all [DOT] agree that he should be suitably recognized.
I would recommend to the minister that he take this into consideration, and also the fact that such an appointment is necessary and would meet with the desires of the business community and of the bar.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have already said all I could say upon this subject of the admiralty court. I promised the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) that in any event we would have a prompt decision. Perhaps I need hardly add that I have taken a note of the very high encomiums passed by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) on our friend Mr. Pentland. I shall treasure up those observations and endeavour to give to each one

its due and proper weight. I had not quite realized that the member could make an appeal to which my heart would be so absolutely responsive as the one he has just made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Yukon Territory, $42,300.

The expenses of the
administration of justice in the Yukon Territory seem to be very high in proportion to the population.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have managed to decrease them $2,000 this year. I think it must be admitted that the administration of justice in the Yukon costs fairly heavily in proportion to the population of the territory, but it must be remembered that we cannot cut down the expenses as the population dwindles. For instance, we have a judge with a fixed salary; and the other expenses are similar. Certainly we are anxious to keep the expenditure within the limits of what will "carry on" the territory, but we must "carry on."
I think, we should not let the minister run away with the credit for the decrease in the expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want any
credit.

It would be illuminating to the committee to consider that it is more the good character of the population of the Yukon Territory which is responsible for the decreased expenditure by $2,000, for that decrease has taken place in the item for the maintenance and transport of prisoners, and I would imagine that the number of prisoners has dwindled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And that decrease in
the number of prisoners is attributable to the excellent system of government under which crime has disappeared. Surely there can be no higher tribute to the Government.

If the right hon. gentleman
takes it in that light, that the increase or the decrease in the number of prisoners is closely related to the good or bad character of the Government, it may be dangerous for him, for we might point out that according to the judical statistics the number of prisoners who are now in our jails has greatly increased as compared with the number there in 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will give an explanation of that when the time arrives.

I know the minister has
always a good explanation to offer-at least
apparently. However, I quite appreciate the explanation given by the right hon. gentleman in this instance, that the cost of administration of justice is not only dependent on the population, but also is dependent to a considerable extent on the area of the territory to be administered.

I notice a big item for
the transportation of prisoners. Is there no jail in the Territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that
prisoners are detained in the Mounted Police establishments, which in the Yukon Territory, as in fact in any unorganized territory, generally serve the purposes of jails.

I notice that this item
includes the maintenance and transport of prisoners. Have we gone back to transportation days? Have we any local Botany Bay? What is meant by "transport of prisoners?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Just what is meant by the transportation the hon. gentleman pays for-but I suppose he does not pay for it- when he comes from Montreal to Ottawa.
Is the second item, living allowance of Judge, $5,000, in addition to his regular salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The judge has a salary of $5,000, and in addition has a living allowance of $5,000. That allowance has been attached to the position ever since it existed. I may say that until a few years ago we had three judges in the Yukon, each at a salary of $5,000 and a living allowance of the same amount, but we arranged, quite a number of years ago, with the reduction of business, to reduce them to one. It will be noticed that the salary of this judge is considerably less than the salary of High Court judges in other provinces; against that he has his allowance of $5,000.

Do the officers of the court
and the police magistrate receive a living allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The police magistrate
receives $1,400 as a living allowance; the other officers receive $1,800.
Is the travelling allowance for the judge paid to him whether he travels or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; he sends in his
bill, just as any other judge does, for his travelling expenses.

How much did he get
last year for travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that he got nothing. Dawson and White Horse are the only two places where judicial business (is required to be carried on. In fact, the judicial business of the Yukon is not very extensive. We keep a judge there not because there is work, but because, of course, we owe it to that population, small as it may be, to provide means for the administration of justice.

The minister has said
that the salary of the judge is $5,000. On page 13 of the Estimates the salary of the judge, territorial court, Yukon territory, is given as $7,000, an increase of $2,000 over the preceeding year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, that is
merely for information; the salaries are settled by the statute. I may say that the judge waited on me last week to represent the grave injustice he had been subjected to because his salary had not been increased. At the moment, however, I cannot find any provision in last session's statute increasing the salary of the judge of the Yukon. I think it must be an error in this statement-which, of course, is not, properly speaking, in the Estimates; it is information as to what is to be paid under statute. However, I will make certain and let my hon. friend know.
I understood the minister to say that the judges are paid travelling allowance according to the actual mileage travelled. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not a matter of
mileage. The judge is entitled to his transportation expenses, to $6 as a living allowance for every day he serves elsewhere than at the place he is by law to live, if that place is not a city, and $10 a day if it is a city. They do not send mileage bills; they set forth what were the transportation expenses incurred, how many days they were away, and where they were.

I find
