in the Auditor General's report that the net sum of $500 was in a great many cases paid for travelling allowance last year. I was wondering how it would work out at $500 in all these cases if the amount of the account depended upon the number of days that the judge served while travelling about.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will find that these are district court judges of Ontario who, I believe, receive a fixed allowance of $500.
Do they get it whether they travel or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it is provided by statute.

How can the Auditor
General get over that? How can $500 be paid to a judge for travelling when he does not travel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Parliament thought
that in view of the conditions in these districts the judges ought to receive that allowance, and we pay what Parliament has said they ought to be paid.
Have these judges passes on the Government railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no information, but I should think not.

It is quite true that the expenditure authorized by statute covers the salary of the judge in the Yukon Territory, but it seems to me that before we vote the item in respect to the living allowance of the judge, we should be quite positive as to the exact amount of his salary under the statute. I do not object to this gentleman getting $7,000; I think he should get it; but if he gets $7,000 a year as his salary, I would be inclined to think at first sight that his living allowance could be reduced. With $7,000 a year of salary, $5,000 for living allowance, and $500 for travelling expenses, that gentleman would get $12,500, that is to say, $2,500 more than the Chief Justice of Quebec or the Chief Justice of Ontario, and $3,500 more than judges of the superior court or the high courts of justice, or the Court of King's Bench in Quebec. I would not be absolutely definite on the point; but if it is the intention of the minister, as the item would indicate, to increase the salary of this gentleman to $7,000, I would like to study this item of living allowance a little further.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The printing of what was intended to be a copy taken from the statute is no indication whatever of any intention in my mind. I would not propose to alter a judge's salary by vote of Parliament. We are not going to vote that $7,000; we are not going to say anything about it. I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that, if this gentleman had $7,000 a year of salary, he ought not to have $5,000 of living allowance. I am practically positive that that $7,000 is an error, and I am quite prepared to assure the hon. gentleman that, if this item goes through

I shall verify the fact and if there be any doubt about it, I shall see that a correction is made. I may say that my practical certainty about the matter results from the fact that, within the last week, I have been waited on by the judge urging me to make his salary $7,000 and his living allowance $3,000, and I think the judge would know if his salary was already $7,000.
What is the interest of the hon. gentleman then to urge the minister to introduce a change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If his salary was $7,000 and his living allowance $3,000, the gentleman is of an age to begin to look forward to a cessation of his usefulness, and his pension would be based upon his salary, not including his living allowance.
And it would be fair?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so.
What is the living allowance of the police magistrate under the item $6,800?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: In addition to his statutory salary of $4,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-expenses of litigated matters conducted within the Department of Justice, $13,000.
What is this amount for when we have so many lawyers in the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is not to pay
lawyer's fees at all. This is to carry on litigation which is not litigation which pertains to particular departments and which, of course, we carry on, but the payment of the expenses of which is provided by the other departments. This is for whatever litigation we have to carry on on behalf of the Government which is not chargeable to any other department. It may be that, in cases where we have to retain lawyers on the outside, their fees are paid out of this appropriation. Last year we spent $7,655 for this purpose; the year before, $1,259, and in 1917-18, $5,146. The amount varies from year to year. For a long number of years past we have inserted the same amount in the Estimates.
What is the meaning of the expression "within the Department of Justice"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand it would cover items such as this: When applications are made to the Privy Council, we have to provide money to pay counsel who appear to make answer; or when we have occasion to send counsel over, when the matter is conducted by the deputy minister himself, as in many instances it is, where we have no outside counsel, we have to provide for expenses of that kind for carrying on litigation which the department-I was mistaken in referring to outside lawyers- carries on without the assistance of outside lawyers. There is always, in carrying on litigation, expense other than the payment of fees to lawyers.
Do I understand the minister to say that none of that amount goes towards paying fees to lawyers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to say absolutely whether it would include any payment to an outside lawyer, but the general nature of the expenditure is what I have indicated, that is, the expense that arises in connection with litigation which is being carried on in the department itself.
Would the minister point out to us in the Auditor General's Report the expenditure of $7,655 which was incurred last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be rather difficult.
Or give us details of the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be very glad to get the details, item by item, for the hon. gentleman if he is interested in them.

Might it be proper on this item to suggest to the minister the advisability of limiting as much as possible appeals to the Privy Council? Of course, sometimes the Department of Justice will be the respondent and will have to follow the litigant wherever he goes, but in other cases the department may be the appellant. Might I point out to the minister what I am sure is quite unnecessary, that appeals to the Privy Council constitute a depressing element upon our Supreme Court. Our Supreme Court can never rise to the position which the Supreme Court of a nation should occupy so long as it is not the court of final result for the nationals of that nation.

I am in thorough accord with what my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has said on this matter. The Supreme Court is a child of our own creation and it does seem to me that the Government ought to see that the child it

has created should be treated with proper dignity and respect. We, at least, ought to be satisfied with the decision of the highest court we have created. I concur with every word my hon. friend has said with respect to that.
Does the item on page L-118 in the Auditor General's Report, litigated matters, $7,635, apply to this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This must be the vote, because that is the exact amount of which I have a note here as having been spent last year.
I also see this: Exchequer Court of Canada, law stamps, $800. Do I understand this to mean that the Department of Justice when they have litigation pay the law stamps to the Exchequer Court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we pay just like any other litigant.
I understand that the law stamp is a tax. Now, kings and sons of kings pay no tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman know that the different departments pay customs taxes on what they import? We pay our law tax just as anybody else pays it. It comes around in the end, I fancy, to the same pocket, but just the same we pay it.
Then it amounts to the King paying taxes. That is an unsound principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall communicate with His Majesty and ask him whether he feels badly about it.

I should imagine it is a mere question of book-keeping between departments. At the same time it is an expense to the Government, as my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) has pointed out, to pay customs brokers for passing entries for the different departments. That appears to me to be extravagance, and a work of supererogation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend will get after the Minister of Trade and Commerce on that subject.
We will.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Annual contribution to the Canadian Law Library, London, England, $500.
Where is that library?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is in connection with the office of the Judicial Committee of the

Privy Council. There is maintained there a law library for the use of Canadian counsel, and we have for a long time paid this annual contribution towards its upkeep.
That would be saved if appeals to the Privy Council were done away with.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.
Are there any further items under the heading "Miscellaneous"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not find any. Call Item 35.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman if he does not think that a nation which has attained full nationhood, as Canada has, should dispense with appeals to the insular tribunal of England?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will have to give me a little while to take in the full effect of the description of the tribunal as "insular." That may make a very great difference. I would just call the attention of the hon. gentleman to this fact, that the jurisdiction of his Majesty's Judicial Committee continues to exist because this Parliament thinks it ought to exist. When the Parliament of Canada makes up its mind that there will be no more appeals from the Supreme Court to the Judicial Committee, there will not be any more appeals, and when the legislatures of the provinces make up their minds that they do not want appeals from their ultimate court of appeal to the Judicial Committee, there will, as I understand it, be no more appeals. I have never been able to understand why people had to use adjectives like "insular" and others more or less flattering, to express what seems to be in their minds-a sort of resentment of the existence of a jurisdiction which exists because the people of Canada are willing it should exist.

The minister has not
answered my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. gentleman that there is no item before the committee, and that a debate upon the abolition of appeals to the Privy Council would certainly not be in order upon the Estimates which we have just disposed of.

May I point out to the Chairman that we were discussing item number 296, and if the committee has passed it I must have missed the Chairman's intimation to that effect. The Chairman was

very quick indeed in passing that item, because so far as I am concerned I never heard the judgment of the committee 1o the effect that it had been voted. If it has not been voted, as I believe, I submit that I am quite within the rules, when discussing a grant to a library near the Privy Council, to speak of that institution itself. I await the ruling of the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item was certainly passed and declared "carried" by the Chair.
Nobody heard it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Justice was further asked what would be the next item called, and after looking through the list he asked me to call item 35. I think the other members of the committee are all aware of that fact.
I would like to call the attention of the Chairman to the fact that before passing an 'item, the question should be put to the committee. I do not believe the question was put on this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have already stated to the hon. member that the question was put to the committee and the item was declared carried.

I might point out to the Chairman that on the next item I shall watch for that feature.
Penitentiaries, $1,371,60,0.
I see that large increases are provided for the penitentiaries, especially in connection with the province of Saskatchewan.
It is a reflection on the province.

It would appear to me that some explanation why the expenditure has increased so greatly in the province of Saskatchewan is due to the committee, in view of the character and demeanour in this House of the representatives from that province, which somehow gives one the idea of respectability, honesty, and other virtues.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are two explanations, neither of which reflects upon the virtue of the province of Saskatchewan. We have made Saskatchewan the scapegoat, having laid upon her the sins of the province of Alberta in the matter of penitentiaries, so that she is now carrying a double burden of fault. That was done for motives of economy, as I think everyone will realize. We can carry on, with overhead
expenses of one penitentiary, much more economically than if we had two institutions to the same number of persons. In addition to that there have been very considerable necessary improvements to the penitentiary buildings themselves at Saskatchewan. If hon. gentlemen will turn to the details which are given immediately underneath they will see wherein there are increases. There are increases in salaries and retiring allowances, attributable, in the first place, to the reclassification, and in the second place, to the fact that we have a larger number of officers because the number of convicts, if not double what it was, has very largely increased. In the item "Lands, buildings, and equipment" there is an increase of some $60,000, all of it rendered necessary, as I am instructed, and as I have reason to know, from work that has been going on for some time, by the necessity of enlarging the accommodation afforded by these buildings.

Has there been any great
increase within the past year in the number of convicts as compared with previous years? If so, what is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the western provinces there is no increase in the sum total of criminals. In the eastern provinces though, I am sorry to say, we have an increase of between 70 and 80 per cent in our penitentiary population. At Kingston I believe the increase is 70 per cent.

Between 70 and 80 per
cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was in error in that respect. Taking the entire eastern part of the country the increase would be about 48 per cent.
What is the nature of the crimes for which the prisoners have been sentenced?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand they are very largely crimes of violence, in which there has been an increase.
Can the minister state the increase in crimes for the province from which we both come?
Is it a crime to come from that province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The superintendent
tells me that a year ago the penitentiary population of St. Vincent de Paul was 465; it is now 554.

Probably there has been
an increase in population.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is an increase
of 89 prisoners in the total number.
What about Dorchester?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The increase there is from 229 to 336.
Can the minister give us the number of prisoners confined in the respective penitentiaries?
Where is Dorchester?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In New Brunswick; it serves the three Maritime Provinces. The convicts in the various penitentiaries are as follows: St. Vincent de Paul, 554; Kingston, 722; Manitoba, 195-which is chargeable partly to Alberta-Saskatchewan, 194; British Columbia, 142 [DOT] and Dorchester 336. These figures are as at the last day of last month.
What is the cost per head of these convicts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Including all expenditures, such as buildings and every other sort of outlay, it is figured that the convicts cost $1.61 per head per day.
What has become of the property of the Alberta penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The surface rights of the property are still owned by the Government. There are valuable mining rights in the property, such as coal deposits, which mining rights have been disposed of. We called for tenders for the sale of the property, but the prices were not satisfactory, and we are confident that the part of wisdom is to wait until a better opportunity offers rather than to try to sell now.
What has been done with the buildings themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The buildings In part have been removed, the materials having been found valuable for use in other penitentiaries. I am told that we utilized in that way for other purposes $185,000 worth of material, all turned to good account.

Were the buildings
demolished?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have not all been destroyed. One of the cell blocks was demolished and the material carefully taken out preserved for use elsewhere, thus being of greater advantage to us than it would be if we tried to sell it. The demand in the market for penitentiary buildings is not particularly great.
I understand that the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary convicts are working overtime at election ballot boxes. Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not heard that they were working overtime.
Well, devoting all their time to this work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Penitentiary labour has been utilized, I believe, in the making of ballot boxes, at the instance of the Chief Electoral Officer.
Will those boxes be used shortly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We expect they will be used in the temperance referendum.

What is allowed each
prisoner in the way of discharge expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that each man on discharge gets $10, with transportation expenses to the place from which he came. Besides this, he gets a suit of clothes, including an overcoat.
Are those clothes made in the institution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Are the clothes made in the penitentiaries sold outside?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, we do not sell anything outside.
Who is the present warden of the Dorchester penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. William Meighen.
Was he recommended by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. He was appointed through the Civil Service Commission and by promotion.
What articles are manufactured in the Kingston penitentiary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand the men
are instructed in practically all the trades- mason work, stone cutting, carpentering, tailoring, boot and shoe making, blacksmith-ing, machine work. They also bake bread, do quarrying work, and carry on farming on a very extensive scale. We do our utmost to furnish them with employment of as diversified a kind as is possible.
When did the vacancy occur in Dorchester penitentiary to which Mr. Meighen was appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think at the beginning of March about a year ago.

When was the appointment
made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It took some little
time I think as the mills of the gods grind slowly.

It would be better for the
minister to say "the mills of the lords." ~

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At all events regardless of whose mills they are they do not grind as fast as they might. I believe it was in June that the finished product was turned out.
Who occupied the post prior to that appointment, and what was the cause of the vacancy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Pipes occupied the position and he was retired on account of failing health.

Was anything paid to him
in the way of an honorarium, and if so, how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He was paid the
gratuity to which he was entitled ifnder the provisions of the statute.
How much was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I believe $6,000 was
the amount. He had been for a lengthy period of years in the service.
Was there no superannuation allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Was he retired at his own
request?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He resigned.
Upon request?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, his state of health was such that he would naturally want to retire.

Was he not requested to
retire by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think when it became quite evident that his health was not such as to enable him to properly per-
6 p.m. form his duties, the officers of the department in the discharge of their duty would call his attention to the fact. I think that was done.

I should have thought he
would have realized that himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had as much to do with public employees as some other people have he would not be so willing to assume that a man is always ready to recognize when the days of his usefulness have gone by.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not referring
to some people who have a sure and certain knowledge of the general public demand. I am talking about gentlemen who are occupying salaried positions, and we find there is not a terrible readiness on their part to come forward and say "I am not as well as I used to be."

I quite agree with my hon.
friend. I have not had the long experience that he has had, but if his experience were mine I would be willing to retire when people wanted me to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no doubt the
hon. gentleman would, but I think he would be surprised to learn just how soon the people would want him to retire.

That is the way with my
right hon. friend.
Mr: FIELDING:	How would the minister define the difference between the dismissal of an officer and a demand for his resignation? What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well I should not say
there would be any very material difference between the dismissal of an officer and a demand for his resignation; but an intimation, or rather a suggestion, to an officer that in view of his condition of health it would be proper for him to retire, seems to me to differ from a demand for his resignation.

It is a case where a
wink is as good as a nod.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must say that I think that the officer in charge would be sadly failing in his duty if he did not call the attention of an official who was breaking down in health to the fact that it would be better for him to resign. I think it would be only the part of kindness not to leave such official there until the person in authority felt compelled to dismiss him, leaving him without any opportunity to obtain what the law intended him to attain when, owing to broken down health, his usefulness has ceased.

There is a regulation shortening the time of prisoners in the peni-

tentiary. What is the nature of that regulation and how does it work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Roughly speaking a
man with a fairly long sentence may gain about one-third of his time. If my memory serves me, during the first six months a man earns six days in the month of remission of his sentence until he has completed seventy-two days. After that he may earn ten days in the month. I think the system works satisfactorily and it is an incentive to good conduct. A man who misbehaves is liable to have so much of his remission struck off, and I think perhaps a strong motive working on the mind of the prisoner is the desire to shorten the period of his imprisonment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No, the item had better
stand until after six o'clock, we have some other matters to bring forward in regard to it.
At six o'clock the committee rose and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Mr. Fripp:
that the House go into Committee on Bill No. 15, to incorporate the North American Trust Company of Canada, and recommending that the title he changed to "An Act to incorporate the Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada."-Mr. Mowat.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in regard to the first Bill on the Order Paper, number 15, to incorporate the North American Trust Company of Canada, I would ask either that the Bill stand over or that it be referred back to the Committee on Private Bills in regard to a change of name. As the House will see, the name of the company incorporated under this Bill is the Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada. Obviously, there is a difficulty in that name; but besides that there is a company doing business in Canada at the present time known as the Scottish Trust Company. That company desires to be heard, and states that it had no notice of this proposed change of name, because the Bill, as originally introduced, provided a name for the new company of the North American Trust company. That, however, 
has been changed by the Private Bills Committee to the name now appearing on the Order Paper, namely, the Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada. As the Scottish Trust Company had no notice of the change and desires to be heard, I think the Bill should be referred back to the Private Bills Committee for further consideration, and I would so move.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I would point out to
the minister that the motion before the House is, that I do now leave the Chair for the House to resolve itself into Committee of the Whole. Action on the specific Bill will have to be in Committee of the Whole, and it would not be competent at this stage to refer it back to the Private Bills Committee. I have no doubt that the Order can stand.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the Bill-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill No. 3 to incorporate the Canadian Bar Association. -Mr. Jacobs.
On the preamble:

I expressed my disapproval of this Bill before the Private Bills Committee, and I want to repeat my objection. I do not think the Canadian Bar Association should be allowed to use this title. We have our bar associations in the various provinces and the members of those associations are precluded from practising law outside their own province. So although I might be a member of this Canadian Bar Association I would [have the 'right to practise law only in my own province. Therefore the name is a misnomer. I do not discuss in any way the objects of the association, I think probably they are commendable, and I am only opposed to the Bill on the ground that an association with such a name would apparently entitle members to practise anywhere in the Dominion, whereas such would not be the case. The name might be changed to the Association of Provincial Bars of Canada. I think the Committee will appreciate that my objection is well founded, as the practise of the law in Canada is a matter of provincial right. There can be no such thing as a Canadian Bar Association according to our law, and therefore I think that this Bill should be referred back to the Private Bills Committee in order that some other name may be given to the association.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think everybody will agree with the hon. gentleman that the different bars are provincial in their organization and scope, but that they do not designate themselves by the name "association." I do not think the adjective "Canadian" as applied to this association is intended to be applied for the purpose of designating that there is a Canadian Bar; but it is applied to the association, which is a bar association solely because it is composed of members of the various provincial bars of this country. In other words, it is an association of Canadian lawyers. It is to be borne in mind that although this association is now being incorporated, it has been in existence for a number of years past and has become known under that name, without conveying to any one the idea that it has any pretension of creating a Canadian bar. The provisions of the Bill itself make it perfectly clear that a bar society is not being created in the sense in which we have those societies in each of the provinces; but rather an association is to be incorporated to which all members of our provincial bars are eligible, and it is in that sense, and in that sense only, that it is called a bar association. I do not think any evil can come to us as members of the provincial bars because we recognize the existence of a Canadian association composed of the members of all those bars. The association is certainly doing excellent work for the profession in particular and for Canada as a whole in bringing together from all the provinces representative members of the profession. These men get together in this association and discuss on the plane of our common Canadian interests matters that particularly pertain to the profession. It seems to me that perhaps the hon. gentleman is a little too apprehensive of the possible meaning that might be attached to the name of this association. I think the Committee should hesitate before depriving this recognized association of the name by which it has been known, and for which it has earned a very creditable reputation, and a name that I think Canadian lawyers as a whole would like to continue to be attached to the association which they have formed, composed of lawyers without distinction of the different bars to which they belong.

I am of the opinion of
the right hon. Minister of Justice. I think the objections of my hon. friend from Labelle are not well founded.
In the English provinces the name "Bar" has not the same signification that it has in Quebec. I understand that in Quebec the Bar is the body that regulates the admission to the study and practice of law; in Ontario we do not use the word "Bar" in that sense. The corresponding institution in that province is the Law Society of Upper Canada, a very old organization, dating from 1792. If we adopt the title suggested by the member for Labelle, it might be mistaken for some other bars which have been abolished in the different provinces. A Canadian Bar Association was formed about twenty jfive years ago, and has since carried that name. I submit that the objection made by my hon. friend is not well founded and that there should be no change in the name.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Preamble agreed to.

I rise to a point of order. I do not find a copy of the Bill on my file, and I cannot get it. I note further that it is not printed in French. I ask therefore, that the consideration of the Bill be deferred until the rules are complied with.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member in charge of the Bill may consent to its being allowed to stand, but as a strict matter of right I must say that any objection to the fact that the Bill is not printed in both languages must be raised before the second reading of the Bill.
Under what rule, please?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The rule asked for by the hon. member from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) will be found on page 508 of Bouri-not. It reads as follows:
The letters E.F. on the Order Paper will show whether that has been done. If any objection be made on that ground, it will prevent the Bill being taken up for its second reading on that day. But if the motion has been made and the debate allowed to proceed thereon, it will be too late then to raise an objection as to the printing in French.

I really think that the Bill has been printed in French; as a matter of fact, I saw a copy of it in the Private Bills Committee. But that reminds me of another objection I have to make. In the French translation the Bill reads "bill pour incorporer la 'Canadian Bar Association'." I think that the name also should be translated so as to read, "L'Association du Bar-reau Canadien."
Bill reported read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House in committee on Bill No. 14, respecting Gilmour and Hughson, Limited, and recommending that title be changed to "An Act to amend an Act to incorporate Gilmour and Hughson, Limited"-Mr. Fripp.
Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-distribution of purchase money and interest ratified.

Would it be in order for the hon. member in charge of the Bill to give some explanation at this time of the reasons why this matter should be brought before Parliament in the form of a Bill instead of being dealt with in the usual way, through the department of the Secretary of State?

This Bill simply asks that the Dominion Act respecting Gilmour and Hughson Limited be amended to allow the shareholders to distribute among themselves a certain sum of money which they have received in part payment for the sale of their assets. Gilmour and Hughson have sold all their limits and assets to the Rior-don Company and have been paid $500,000 on account. Nobody is interested in this sum except the two families, the Gilmours and the Hughsons; there are no creditors. It is simply asking Parliament to amend their Act so that the moneys may be distributed among those entitled to them as they are paid in, and until the purchase is finally concluded. The purchase price can only be paid out under the proposed legislation by the unanimous consent of all the shareholders, and, as I have intimated, there are no shareholders except the two families.
Was that Bill not before the committee yesterday and deferred for further consideration?
No, the Bill was in committee yesterday and thoroughly discussed and, as it now appears, was unanimously approved.
I do not quite understand the hon. member's explanation. Why is special legislation necessary in this case? Could not these moneys be distributed without special legislation?

The distribution of the
assets cannot be made under the original Act unless the company is wound up. They do not want to apply for a winding-up order, because if they did, they would be asking for something that might be very

injurious to them if all the payments of purchase money were not made in due course, the only way that they can distribute the first instalment of $500,000 amongst the shareholders is by having their Act amended giving them that power. That is all they are asking for by this Bill.
The hon. member assures the committee that there is no objection to the Bill from any interested party?
None whatever.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Preamble agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is a recommendation from the committee-this can, of course, only be carried out on the third reading-that the title of the Act be changed to "An Act to amend an Act to incorporate Gilmour and Hughson Limited."
Bill reported, and read the third time.
Mr. FRIPP moved that the said Act do now pass and that the title thereof be "An Act to amend an Act to incorporate Gilmour and Hughson, Limited."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Bill No. 24 for the relief of Frank Alexander Staunton.-Mr. Smith.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Penitentiaries, $1,371,600.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at six o'clock, the Estimates of the Department of Justice were under consideration. We had reached item No. 35, penitentiaries, $1,371,600. The item had been discussed, but the discussion had not yet terminated.

I notice quite a large increase amounting in all to $275,000, the increases going all through the different penitentiaries. Can the minister give some details in regard to the Maritime penitentiary situated at Dorchester? For instance, the first item, salaries and retiring allowances, amounts to $83,000 this year, whereas, last year it was $60,000. What is the reason for the increase? How many officials are in the institution and what are their salaries? How many have retired?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The increase is attributable to the classification. The classification affects not merely the amount of salary, but the amount of retiring gratuity,

the retiring gratuity consisting of a certain number of monthly payments, I think a month for each year that a man has served, but based on his average salary for the the three years preceding his retirement. Thus an increase in salary means also an increase in gratuity to those retiring, and the increase in this particular penitentiary is almost entirely attributable to this cause.

Has the minister a list of
those proposed to be retired during the coming year who will come under this? An increase of $28,000 for one institution is very large.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As regards retirements that may happen in the future, we can proceed only by an estimate; we cannot say now in advance that a certain man will be retired during the coming year. If we did, that man might die before he was due to retire.
Of shock?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We do not retire people indiscriminately at a fixed age. A man's retirement depends upon his usefulness. If he breaks down so that he cannot be useful to the penitentiary, we will retire him. There may be men to-day in possession of all their faculties and capacities-we cannot determine in advance that they may have to be retired-but in the course of a year they may fail. We can proceed only by making an estimate based upon past experience of what we anticipate will be required for that purpose.

Is that item of $50,000 for
lands, building and equipment, for the purchase of land, or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does not include the acquisition of any land; it is for the completion of a new cell wing, the installation of proper waterworks, and the maintenance of the necessary building repairs.

I understand the Government in the past bought a large farm adjoining this penitentiary and that the convicts are working on it, cultivating it, daily during the summer season. Has this farm been a paying proposition during the last few years? What kind of crops are grown? Are cattle raised? What is the income from the farm?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The income from this
farm last year was $21,000. If we take the penitentiaries as a whole, the value of the products of last year, taken at ordinary wholesale prices, was some $94,000. I think
we have every reason to recognize that our farming operations have been carried on to advantage.
How many acres does the farm comprise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
About 900 acres at
Dorchester. I am told most of it is marsh land; it is not all available for cultivation.
The minister told us this afternoon that in the Kingston Penitentiary the number of inmates was 722. What staff of officials and employees is required to take care of those inmates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The permanent staff
at Kingston penitentiary is at present 98.

Are the various supplies
necessary for the maintenance of the penitentiary purchased by tender? Let me cite a few items: woollen from the Amherst Woollen Mills, Truro, $5,639. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Tenders are asked fot and the purchasing is supervised by the Purchasing Commission. In this particular instance, tenders were asked for.

Was the contract awarded
to the lowest tenderer?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand contracts are always awarded to the lowest tenderer. The purchasing is done under the control and direction of the Purchasing Commission.
And the minister is responsible to Parliament so far as that commission is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I take my responsibility for the purchasing, and I am assured that in this instance, as in all instances, the contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer.
Were tenders also called for in connection with that item of $4,523, purchased from the Canadian Cottons at Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am told that tenders were called for in that case that in fact they are called for in the case of all purchases, the calls being sent out by our own purchasing agent under the direction of the Purchasing Commission.
How are they called?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The forms are sent
out under the direction of the Purchasing Commission.
To whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
To all those from
whom the Purchasing Commission considers you could expect to purchase goods of the kind.

Has the department purchased any supplies for the penitentiaries from the Militia Department? I see by the newspapers that some distributors in Ottawa, Smith and Carey, for example have blankets, sheets, and comforters for sale, from the Department of Militia. If these could be supplied to the penitentiaries, they would not cost as much as if they were bought from the wholesale merchants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have had quite
a number of articles transferred from the Militia Department and from the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, without payment, of course, the goods belonging to the Government. As the result of the cessation of the war there has been an overplus in the Militia Department of some goods, and where there has been an overplus of articles in any department that we required for the penitentiaries we have had them transferred to us.

By what authority is
the Purchasing Commission operated?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Purchasing Commission as I explained this afternoon, is operating under an Order in Council providing for the supervision and direction of the purchasing operations of the different departments. There has been some contusion-I do not know whether the hon. gentlemen has that same thing in his mind -between the Purchasing Commission so operated, and the Purchasing Commission which existed with special powers under the War Measures Act. The present commission is a commission appointed by the Governor in Council to supervise the general purchasing operations of the different departments, so that there may be one common direction.

I do not wish to get into a discussion about the Purchasing Commission, but I have a recollection of an attempt to pass legislation in this House in two previous sessions creating a purchasing commission, and I merely wish to know if this present commission has been foisted on the public by Order in Council after it had been refused by Parliament. Is it the same commission, the same personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a body with quite different powers. The Purchasing Commission which it was proposed to constitute by statute would have been a body exercising

authority and power under the direct statutory enactment of this Parliament. The present Purchasing Commission is purely a body appointed by Council-Council having the supervision of the purchasing of all the departments-to exercise a power of supervision and direction over the purchasing operations of the departments generally. It is quite a different body from what was contemplated under the proposed statute which never was enacted. If the hon. gentleman will carry his memory back he will remember that Parliament voted a special sum of money to provide for the expenses of this purchasing body, the explanation I am giving now having been given at that time.

Is the personnel of the
present commission the same as that of the other commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The personnel of the
present body is not the same as the personnel of the Purchasing Commission under the War Measures Act.
Would the minister cite the statutory power which the Government had to pass such an Order in Council appointing such a commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can give no specific statutory power that we had to do that, but the Government has not only the power but the duty to administer the business of the country, and each one of the departments makes its purchases subject to its responsibility to the Government. The entire Government is responsible for the operations of each department. That being so, it was thought wise to appoint a body that should endeavour to co-ordinate these different operations and see that some common principle ran through them all, but the entire power of that body is the power of the Governor in Council. Its functions are to assist the Governor in Council in carrying out that part of its duty of administering the public affairs which involves seeing that the purchasing is done, so far as possible, under the best circumstances.

But the right hon. gentleman will not tell this House that the Governor in Council has the right to appoint a commission without statutory power, general or specific? What I wish to know is: what general or specific power had the Governor in Council to pass the Order in Council referred to by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I tried to make clear, but evidently did not succeed-
I understood very clearly *what the right hon. gentleman said, but he did not say everything I wanted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid it would be quite impossible for me, adhering strictly to the truth, to say all the things the hon. gentleman wants me to say. There are some limitations put on a man when he is trying to tell the truth. Perhaps it does not always happen that the hon. gentleman wants to hear what is the truth. As I said, the Governor in Council is responsible, because it is the executive body, for the administration of the public business.
Not responsible to Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, it is responsible to Parliament. I did not conceive it was necessary to add those words. We are responsible to Parliament, and through Parliament to the people of Canada, for the proper administration of the general public business, and part of that business that devolves upon the executive is the purchasing of those things required for the Government. The Government adopts what seems to it the best method of ensuring that that purchasing is properly supervised so that the public interest may be fully taken care of, and it designates certain employees to do that. The mere fact that these people are called a commission does not alter the situation in the slightest. The authority of the Government to select people to do the best they can to see that the purchasing is properly co-ordinated is the inherent authority that necessarily follows from the fact of this duty being the Government's. So far as the constituting of that particular body is concerned, the authority of Parliament was given by the vote of Parliament. Parliament voted the money to provide for the constitution of a body of that kind, and it was explained what the purpose of that commission was.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the
committee understands clearly that the Purchasing Commission, to which my hon. friend is now referring, is acting under a different authority from that which would have been exercised by the commission that would have been appointed under the Bill introduced last session, had that Bill become law. What is the difference between the function and nature of the Purchasing Commission, as appointed under the Order in Council, and those which would have existed under the Bill as drawn last session?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the Bill had been
passed that commission would have been constituted as a statutory body, not dependent upon any particular department, but with functions of its own exclusively. As the matter stands now, it is merely a body of employees whom the Government has designated to supervise the purchasing, and to endeavour to effect the necessary co-ordination so that purchases of similar things for different departments may be made through, and with the co-operation of a body that has knowledge of the requirements in different departments, the knowledge acquired in connection with one transaction being available when dealing with another. The purpose is to establish one common principle that will apply to all departments. The other body, on the other hand, would have had authority of its own. Whereas the present commission acts for the departments, the other body would have been in a sense a distinct department, entitled on its own authority to determine these matters, and to make all purchases. Under the other system, the commission would have been a sort of purchasing department. Here it is a mere committee or commission-the word is immaterial-of officials selected by the Government, to supervise and direct the purchasing of the different departments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister nas made it clear that there may be a difference in names. But what is the difference in function between this commission or committee existing now and the body that would have exercised purchasing power under the Bill had it been passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a difference between servants of departments, and of the united departments as represented by the Government, and a body constituted by Parliament to control purchasing of its own authority. That is the difference. These are the employees of the executive Government, with no functions assigned to them by Parliament exercisable otherwise than under the direction of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has not answered my question yet. He has elaborated on the difference in the nature of the composition of the two bodies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let me make it as
short as I can: The other body was a statutory purchasing authority; this is a body acting under the authority of the Governor in Council, which is charged with

purchasing and responsible for its being done. Now, I do not know whether I have made myself clear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Leaving aside the question of authority, what would the other purchasing body have done, which this particular commission now is not doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It would have exercised that authority to determine matters itself which this body does not do. I am endeavouring to make the positon clear, but the thing is so palpable to me that I cannot understand how there can be any room for misapprehension.
It is as clear as mud to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I am sorry the mud is so thick over there that the light is not able to penetrate. That, however, is not my fault.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let me put the question another way. Are there any purchases which this particular body might make to-day which the other body would not have been authorized to make and, vice versa, would the other body have had power to make certain purchases which this body has not the right to make?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not before me the enumerated powers of the other body, but the substantial distinction is this: the other body would determine what should be bought and how it would go about buying it. It settled those transactions on its own authority. This body supervises the operations of the different departments and co-ordinates them, and its authority begins and ends with the authority of the Governor in Council. It is derived from the Governor in Council. The other body had authority of its own which might operate adversely to the decision of a department. It controlled the purchasing, which was taken as a substantial thing by itself and put into its hands. The present body simply supervises and co-ordinates the purchasing. The provisions of the proposed statute, which was not enacted, intended to create a purchasing commission as a distinct body standing on its own feet.
Were the members of this commission or purchasing body appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; they were not
appointed by the Civil Service Commission, but by Council.

Under what authority
were they appointed by Council without reference to the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They were not under
the Civil Service Act at all.

Apparently they are
under no Act at all except the act of the Government, which is not a very good one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will have to be satisfied with my statement.
What is the personnel of this commission which is purchasing under the authority of the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The commission is at
present composed of Mr. Howard, chairman, and Col. La Fleche.
Only two?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I think the law provided
that the Civil Service Act should of necessity apply to the appointments of all servants either in the inside or outside service. Will the minister tell us how, after passing the Civil Service Act, they can appoint servants of the State, civil servants, without the formality of submitting such appointments to the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These positions are not clerical in the sense of embodying in them civil servants of the country. These men were appointed to exercise particular supervision on behalf of the Governor in Council. It was judged at the time that it was possibly open to the Governor in Council to appoint them to perform these duties, and they were appointed. It did not seem to us that they came under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. If we are open to criticism in that regard, well we will have to consider it from that point of view. Personally, I confess it is the first time it occurred to me that there should be any question with regard to their being appointed by the Civil Service Commission. Perhaps I may be permitted to point out at this stage that we have travelled a very long distance from the estimates for the penitentiaries.

May I answer the right hon. gentleman in this way-that I asked some questions as to how the purchase of certain articles falling under the item we are now considering, that is to say the penitentiaries, was made. The right hon. gentleman told us that the purchase had been made by a commission appointed under an

Order in Council; and I say that we are strictly within the rules of the committee, and are adhering closely to the point, when we put questions to the minister as to the character of the commission. Its personnel, its appointment, and any questions in reference to that commission, are, to my mind strictly in order. Since the right hon. gentleman has told us that the members of that commission were not statutory officials of the Government hut that they were servants of the state-"ordinary servants" to use his very words-I wish to ascertain from him how he can escape from the rule laid down in a statute, sanctioned by this Parliament, which made it obligatory on the part of the Government not to appoint any servants of the state except through the authority of the Civil Service Commission, or by virtue of a special Act. The right hon. gentleman has told us that there was no special statute in this case-that the Government were acting under the general powers which are vested in His Excellency the Governor General in Council and that in the exercise of that authority they had appointed the purchasing commission in question. I want to go a step further and ask my right hon. friend a very simple question: Are there any members of the Civil Service in Ottawa who can be appointed without the authority of a statute and without the authority of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must decline, in advance to go into an enumeration of the powers of all the other departments, but so far as my knowledge goes there are employees who are appointed without the intervention of the Civil Service Commission. Now as to the question of the regularity-
Would the minister be good enough to point out some instances?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With all respect I do suggest that I should not be called upon to enter upon an accounting with respect to other departments than the
9 p.m. one with which I am concerned.
I will be very happy to discuss the general question of the appointment of a purchasing commission, and of the nature of the present one, upon a proper occasion; but I am asking no vote whatever in connection with that body. It is not a body attached to any department in any way-it is a general body appointed for general purposes. My hon. friend and myself seem to have to differ in opinion as to the method by which the commission ought
to be appointed. I have expressed my view upon the subject. It does not meet the approval of the hon. gentleman, and I have to admit that I do not see how I am going to convince him that my view is right. Unfortunately his views differ from mine, and that is all that I can say about it.

There is something further to be said. Is there not an Order in Council which prohibits the Government, in the case of contracts amounting to more than $5,000, from accepting those contracts except upon tender, the tenders to be opened by the minister himself in the presence of the secretary of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not to my knowledge that there exists any such Order in Council. I do understand-
Is there a statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do understand that
there are statutes with regard to certain departments and the purchases to he made by them, but I am not aware that there exists an Order in Council such as the hon. gentleman refers to.
Mr. VIEfl:	Well, let us say a statute
then. Is there not a statute which makes it obligatory for every department of the state not to purchase any articles, or award contracts, for any higher amount than $5,000, except upon tender called for by the department, and opened by the minister himself in the presence of the secretary of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not aware of any such general statute. I believe that there are statutes with regard to specific departments. If my memory serves me, there is a statute containing such a provision with regard to the Marine and Fisheries Department. I think there is a similar statutory provision with regard to the Public Works Department; but I can only say to the hon. gentleman that I, this evening, do not know of such a statute as that to which he refers. Of course I do not pretend to know all the statutes that are in existence. I came here prepared to discuss the Esti mates of my own department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think I can promise to quote the statute in question to my right hon. friend before the evening is over.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of universal application?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, a general statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not denied that there exists such a statute. I have said in reply to the question put to me that at this moment I cannot recall that a general statute exists. However, I am quite fallible; I may be mistaken.

We have perhaps
drifted far afield-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we have.

-but perhaps I can say a word further along that line. Now as to the appointment of these commissioners I do not follow the reasoning of the minister in saying that he, or any other minister, or any department, has inherent power to make appointments. I do not think they have. The Government, and every department of Government, is created by statute. There is no such thing as a minister of common law; there are no common law ministers. They, and every department of Government are created by statute, consequently you must go to the statute to find the powers of a minister or the powers of a department. The statute which created each department governs it; and if it does not give a minister such power, I would say, with all due respect to the minister, that no such power exists at all. Therefore these appointments cannot be made under an inherent power which, in my judgment, does not exist. If there is a statute giving such powers in a general way, then of course there would be the inherent power of carrying out what was incidental to the real purpose of that statute; but we have statutory provisions made with respect to all these departments governing the appointment of a purchasing agent. That statute is supposed to have provided for all that is necessary in each department ; but I cannot agree with the minister that he can go beyond that and create another body for the purpose of having the general supervision of the purchases in all departments. I submit it is irregular for the Government to make such appointments, and in doing so and undertaking to pay salaries to such parties, they are acting utterly without authority.
Could the minister tell us when the commission was appointed under the Order in Council referred to?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is difficult for me to recall the exact date. While I have no desire to unduly limit hon. gentlemen in the discussion, at the same time they should appreciate the fact that this commission was not appointed in my department.

I have not come here prepared to discuss a question of this kind. It may be a very debatable question, and I shall be glad to discuss it at the proper time. If I had had any notice that it was going to be brought up I would have come prepared with these dates and with the terms of the Order in Council itself ready to discuss the reasons why-whether they be sufficient in the eyes of hon. gentlemen opposite or not-it was thought proper for the members of that purchasing commission to be appointed as they were appointed. I shall be glad to look into the whole of the circumstances and to facilitate the further discussion of this matter. But I think hon. gentlemen opposite will appreciate that we cannot get any very satisfactory result in trying to continue this discussion with a minister who avowedly has not come here with the necessary information for which hon. gentlemen very naturally ask.

I only asked the minister in order to get him out of his present dilemma by having him tell us when the purchasing commission was appointed. I understand my hon. friend from Lotbiniere asked a question regarding an item that was purchased in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920. I do not think that this Purchasing Commission was in existence under Order in Council or otherwise at that time. Perhaps the minister can give us a different answer to that which he originally gave, and in that way overcome his difficulty regarding the present Purchasing Commission, which is illegally constituted and is causing him additional worry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very much
obliged to the hon. gentleman for trying to extricate me from my troubles. My recollection is that the commission was appointed in the month of July.
Of what year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The vote was passed
in the last days of the last session of .Parliament, which I think terminated on the 1st July; but I would not undertake to be accurate in that statement.

Will the minister tell us
under what department that Purchasing Commission operates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Commission reports to the Department of Finance.
It is under the Finance Minister then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
So far as it is under
a specific minister, because it is dealing with all the departments.

I quite appreciate the
answer given by the minister a minute ago, which I think was quite fair, that he is not ready to discuss the whole subject of the commission, the right hon. gentleman said also that he had not been given notice of the question; otherwise he would have been prepared to answer fully. I might point out to him that this discussion was absolutely sprung on us by reason of the fact that the minister told us that the purchases under review had been made through that commission. This was all new to us, for the simple reason that the War Purchasing Commission was abolished at the expiration of the War Measures Act. It is true a bill was introduced last session to give the Government power to appoint a permanent purchasing commission, but that bill was withdrawn. Then notwithstanding the fact that Parliament had not granted authority for so doing, we find that a commission was appointed by Order in Council under no statutory powers except the general powers vested in his Excellency in Council. We find moreover that these officials are not statutory officials but that they are servants of the state, although the provisions of the Civil Service Act are flatly in contradiction of the minister as to the powers of the Governor in Council to make appointments to the inside service at Ottawa. But I will not insist further on this point. I think it is only fair to defer the discussion to a later date to enable the minister to get the information of which he stands so much in need tonight, so that when we take up the subject again he may be able to supply the committee with the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will also afford hon. gentlemen an opportunity of discussing the subject with the minister to whom it properly belongs.

Yes. But I think it was only proper that the minister should give this committee some information as to how the purchases are made in his department. I asked him how the purchases were made of some specific items, namely, from Green at Kipgston, amounting to $9,900; from the Amherst Woollen Mills, Truro, $5,639; from Canadian Cottons, Montreal, $4,523; from Canada Cement Company, Montreal, $2,314. The minister has told this committee that these purchases were made through the Purchasing Commission; but a few minutes later, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Pontiac, he replied that the commission had, to the best of his recollection, been appointed in July, 1920. The items to which I refer were for the year ended 31st March, 1920, so that the commission could not have been in existence at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was a previous commission in existence.
Not for those purchases; that was the War Purchasing Commission before.

The right hon. gentleman will not contend that the War Purchasing Commission was functioning up to the 31st March, 1920. If the Purchasing Commission created by Order in Council in July 1920 was not the commission to which he referred, why did he answer the hon. member for Pontiac that the commission had been created by Order in Council of that date? Will the minister tell us something about that previous commission which did the purchasing at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I said before, I am not in a position to give the hon. gentleman the details of these two commissions which succeeded each other.
Was it the War Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A commission was
created under an Order in Council passed by virtue of the War Measure Act. my impression is that that commission continued in existence until the end of the last session. Then a commission was appointed afterwards. I spoke of that subsequently appointed commission in answer to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill); because hon. gentlemen were discussing a commission which, as they represented it, had been created by Order in Council and in spite of the refusal of Parliament to pass a statute. I was talking, therefore, about the particular commission to which they applied that description. As I said before, if the hon. gentleman desires a discussion that will involve the details of the constitution of these different commissions I shall be very glad to enter into that discussion with him, but certainly I do not think that either he or I have under our hands at the present moment the material necessary to make that discussion useful.

I am satisfied for the time
being, Mr. Chairman, I think that this further discussion will not be useless, be-

cause it will enable the right hon. gentleman to produce the information asked for with regard not only to this last commission, but to all previous commissions created by Order in Council or under the War Measures Act. I would like some information as to the purchase from Mc-Kelvey and Birch, of Kingston, of various articles aggregating $9,783, as set out on page L23 of the Auditor General's report. Were tenderers asked in connection with the purchase of these articles, and if so, from whom were tenders received?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I can get the details
of the particular contracts if the hon. gentleman is interested in them, but for the moment the only answer I can give him is that these purchases were made under the system followed in the case of all purchases,-that is, offers were called for, and under the supervision of whichever commission was at the time in existence, the purchases were made from those whose prices were found to be the lowest.

Then I understand that the
purchase was not made directly by the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not in a position to say whether the final purchase was carried out through our purchasing agent with the assent and approval of the commission, or whether it was carried out through an officer of the commission. I shall be very glad to obtain that information for my hon. friend.

In view of the answer
given by my right hon. friend I wish to point out that it is not proper for a minister of the Crown to come before the committee unprepared to give full information concerning expenditure reported by the Auditor General for the previous year. We are now called upon to vote $1,371,000 for the maintenance of penitentiaries. Last year the amount was considerably less. For the Kingston penitentiary the appropriation last year was $71,000 less; for St. Vincent de Paul, $65,000 less; for Dorchester, $49,000 less, and so on. It is with a view to the furnishing of full information that the Estimates of a department are not brought up in the House until the Auditor General's report is laid on the Table. In answer to the leader of the Opposition the other day the Prime Minister clearly stated that no Estimates would be taken up until the report of the Auditor General in respect to the departments concerned had been

brought down. The minister, assisted by his officials on the floor of the House, is supposed to give full information concerning each item set forth in the report. I might commend to the right hon. gentleman the example of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) who gave the fullest particulars concerning his Estimates and who satisfied both sides of the House with the information he furnished, to the point that he got a certificate of ability from the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon).
I will not say that the Minister of Justice is not capable, but I do say that there is a lack of preparation on his part in connection with the presentation of his Estimates which this committee should lay stress on. Now, I should like to ask the minister how the following items were purchased as set forth on page L-23 of the Auditor General's report:	basin cocks, 46
at $1.45; bends, 21 at $1.40; branch headers, 20 at $6.25; brass bolts and nuts, 250 at 15 cents, etc., to the amount of $9,783. I have my suspicions, Sir, that these various items were not purchased by tender. In this case of plumbing supplies it would seem to be better to make the purchases wholesale. If they were purchased wholesale, tenders must have been called.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have already stated that tenders were called for these as they are called for everything. Now, I am at a loss to know in what respect the hon. gentleman finds fault with me for not having the particulars or details. Does he want the papers about each particular purchase? If he is satisfied with a general statement, all of these things were purchased after proper tenders were called for them. No doubt where quantities were large enough to enable us to buy wholesale, we bought wholesale. But if only a couple of taps were wanted, one could not very well go and buy a large enough quantity to make one's order a wholesale order.

In this item, there are pur- -chases amounting to $9,000 from one firm for one penitentiary in one year. It seems to me that those supplies, particularly in view of the fact that1 we have so many penitentiaries, should always be purchased wholesale. When they purchased from McKelvey and Birch in Kingston, hard rubber stops, 603 at $32.25, I have serious doubts that these were purchased by tender. The minister told us a minute ago that purchases were made by tender when the quantities were sufficient to warrant a purchase by wholesale.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I said that we purchased them from wholesalers when the quantity was sufficiently large to make that possible.
Were the tenders opened in the department of the minister or by this "fly-by-night" commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
