speechtext: They are opened in the presence of the Purchasing Commission or their representative, by the purchasing agent of the Department of Justice.
The minister does not attempt to divest himself of responsibility as to purchases made through the Purchasing Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am here carrying full responsibility for the purchases, and nothing is purchased excepting after the requisition has been submitted to me and initialled by the minister. Under the general practice, purchases under $500 may be initialled by the deputy minister; but if the amount is over $500, before the purchase is made, the requisition has to be initialled by the minister, and I have the full responsibility. Tenders are not opened by myself personally. I do not think that was ever done in the Department of Justice, and with the great respect that I have for the positiveness with which certain hon. gentlemen are convinced that they can produce a general statute with the requirements that they have mentioned, I think it will be found that they are mistaken in that regard. The practice that is followed is the practice that has been followed from time immemorial. Everything that we bought and what we paid for it are in the public accounts; the documents in connection with it are absolutely available if any one wants to inquire into them, and certainly they will be readily and willingly produced and subjected to any scrutiny that may be thought desirable. This is the first time that it has been suggested to me that, in not coming myself with, at my finger-ends, the details of each particular purchase that can be found in the Auditor General's Report; I have come showing a very grave lack of preparedness. If I had anticipated that there would be a desire for such detailed information, I would have brought it. I shall see that the hon. gentleman gets it with regard to any item whatever which he thinks calls for further inquiry and, of course, as is the case with the entire Public Accounts, those relating to my department are open to the closest possible scrutiny and investigation in the proper place-before the Public Accounts' Committee.

The minister's long parliamentary experience will tell him that all ministers of the Crown, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Agriculture and the ministers of each of the other departments, always come fully prepared to answer questions put as regards expenditures. I do not want to be obnoxious or unduly annoying to the minister; I am simply pointing out to him that we are now called upon to vote an appropriation of $1,371,600. The information that I seek to obtain is for the purpose of assuring myself that the purchases for these penitentiaries, the requirements of which are practically the same, are done on a general system which would save the department undue expense that would be occasioned by purchases being made at local retail stores. The requirements of all the penitentiaries are practically the same. If the minister's contention is right that these purchases were made through a Purchasing Commission, it does not appear to me that it should be necessary to have all the details that the Auditor General's Report contains, showing separate purchases here and there. I should think that the requirements would be purchased by the commission in large volumes, kept in a central store and given out to the various penitentiaries as required. This expenditure may be largely curtailed by a proper system, but the committee has not been able to ascertain, as a certain fact, whether these articles were purchased through the commission or the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I might quote to the minister the chapter I had in mind, chapter 39 of the Revised Statutes of Canada in relation to Public Works. In the interpretation clause, there is this definition:
"Public work'' or "public works" means and includes any work and property under the control of the minister.
Section 36 reads:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the Government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases,-
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or,
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and' servants of the department; or,
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than $5,000.

That is the section to which I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only works We
have to do in our department are done by the convicts. We do not get public works done for us. We have to get the material to be put into the works, but the works themselves are done by the convicts so that we never have a contract for a public work. These articles that are bought are either for use in the penitentiary or to be Used in the construction work which the convicts carry on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister not regard material he has bought for construction work, as property under his control?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can see no application of that statute to things that are referred to here. You cannot make a public work out of a tap. Amongst things an hon. gentleman mentioned were taps that were purchased, I have no doubt, to be placed in the penitentiary, and the work is all done by the convicts under the supervision of instructors in the different trades within the penitentiary. We never have a contract to give for a public work.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister not regard the spirit of the statute as an instruction given by Parliament in regard to calling for tenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to see
the statute, because there are specific statutes with regard to specific departments. If the hon. gentleman will let me look at the statutes, I think I shall be able to point out to him that it does not apply in the present instance. Here it is; An Act respecting the Public Works of Canada. In this Act.
(a)	'Minister' means the Minister of Public works;
(b)	'Department' means the Department of Public Works;
(c)	'public work' or 'public works' means and includes any work or property under the control of the minister.
That is, under the control of the Minister of Public Works. This is entirely a statute with regard to the public works of Canada, and all the provisions are subject to this definition that 'Minister' means the Minister of Public Works, and that 'public work' or 'public works' means and includes any work or property under the control of the minister. That is, of the Minister of Public Works; the paragraph immediately preceding tells us that. I do not think we need go any further to see that this Act has no application in this case.

There is a statute about the Department of Justice. There is a Penitentiaries Act, which deals with the manner in which penitentiaries are to be carried on, and so far as the statutory law is concerned, those are the statutes that govern the operations of the department. I think the hon. gentleman is quite in error in thinking the word 'Minister' there to mean any minister at all, in view of the fact that we have a definition of what 'Minister' is in this Act. The hon. gentleman will find there are other departments in regard to which an analogous provision about contracts exceeding $5,000 is expressly made. Now if the clause the hon. gentleman cites had the general application he is trying to attach to it there would be no reason for making this provision with regard to other departments. I do not think there is need for me to go any further. The section I have read makes it quite clear. The Act is divided into two parts. Part 1 applies exclusively to public works under the control of the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Part 2 contains the section to which I have referred; that is the point. My right hon. friend will see that Part 2 includes all the departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
has not indicated where in the Act the purchasing of goods is described as a public work, and our contracts are for the purchase of goods.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister will admit that he was mistaken when he Said that this Act was confined to public works.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Part 2 confines its
application in a general way to public works.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To any
department of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But we are not executing any public works at all. We are simply buying goods.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It says:
'public work' or 'public works' means and includes any work or property under the control of the minister. Does the minister say that the material he uses is not property under his control?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But 'Minister' is
specifically defined as being the Minister of Public Works

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is in
relation to Part 1, but not in relation to Part 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Where do you find the
reference in Part 2?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In section 36.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will indicate a case in which this department has been excuting a public work, then we may consider the matter, but our contracts are purchases of goods pure and simple.

Will the minister tell us
which items in the Estimates comprise these purchases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These are the Estimates of what we expect to spend next year. It is not the money that we spent last year that is in these Estimates.

What is covered for example, by the item " working expenses?" In the case of Kingston penitentiary, there is a very large item of $7,000 for working expenses and $25,000 for industries. Just what is meant by that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I believe the largest
single item included in working expenses is the purchase of coal. To carry on a penitentiary, among other things that we have to do is to heat it.

I think that would come
under maintenance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Maintenance refers to
the maintenance of convicts, that is, the feeding of convicts; whether that is the best possible way of expressing it I do not know. The term " working expenses " is used to cover the entire expense of working the penitentiary. I understand that it covers all the supplies, other than the feeding of the convicts, which are necessary to carry on a penitentiary.

What comes under the
heading of industries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Industries are the
works we carry on by which we earn some money. We have made mail bags, for instance.
And ballot boxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We made some ballot
boxes too. We carry on a boot-making industry. We make all the boots for all the convicts and all the officers, as well as all the clothes the convicts and officers wear.
Are any of these industries revenue producing?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We make no sales outside the penitentiaries, except certain things we have made for the use of the Government. We have repaired mail bags, for instance, and have made some clothing for the Indian Department.
What is the limitation of the purchasing power of the superintendent of the penitentiary? Can he purchase directly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The superintendent
has no purchasing power.
The local authorities cannot purchase anything directly?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In an emergency they
may purchase something that is absolutely called for at the moment, in the case for instance of a bursting pipe or something of that kind, but they have no general purchasing power. The purchasing is done through the department here.

I should like to illustrate
the argument I put forward a moment ago as to the advisibility of having a central system'of purchasing for the penitentiaries. For instance, if the minister will look at page 123, he will find that he purchased 1,200 bags of flour from the Lake of the Woods Milling Company at $5.40 per bag, and he purchased also six hundred bags of flour from McBroom, Kingston, at $6.35. So that there was a difference of 95 cents . a bag between these two purchases of flour. I will not bother the minister for details because he is not in a position to give them, but he will see that there is apparently a lack of system in purchasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be, and there may not. You buy what you require at the time you require it, or at the time you think you can purchase to the best advantage, and I have no doubt that these purchases were made at what was considered the most opportune and advantageous time. The purchasing agent has to use his judgment as to the best method of making purchases. Would the hon. gentleman suggest that it would have been better for us to have bought all that flour at the time we paid $6.35? As a matter of fact, it turned out that some other day we were able to purchase flour at $5.40. We have to exercise our best judgment in purchasing, and it may therefore be wiser at a certain time to buy a limited quantity, looking forward to being able to buy on a greater scale to better advantage later on. I am not myself an expert in matters of this kind, but I am advised by those who are

experts tliat the best way to obtain the final, general, good result is to entrust someone who is competent to exercise good judgment as to the best time to lay in your supply. That we have done, and I am satisfied that the general results would convince the hon. gentleman that our purchasing has been done to the best advantage.

I quite appreciate the argument of the minister, but as regards the system of purchasing, I think he might give us some further enlightenment. I admit that it may be advisable to purchase a limited quantity when prices are excessive, but what I should like to know is just how this purchasing is done. The minister told us that it was done by his department, either through the purchasing agent, or through the commission; he did not know. However, we shall probably have occasion to come back to this question when the commission is under fire.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The modus operandi is this: When they require certain articles at a penitentiary, they forward their requisition to the superintendent, who looks into it and passes it if he finds that the requirements are justifiable.	.
Do they do that periodically, every three or six months, or every month?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For things with which they require to be supplied for long periods, they do, such, for instance, as groceries and meats that are a matter of steady supply. Of course, there are some things they require one year and not another. At all events, as supplies are required, and as they anticipate the wants of the institutions, so far as they can be anticipated in things of the kind I have spoken of, they forward their requisition to the superintendent. He passes judgment upon it from the point of view of its propriety, and he then submits it to the purchasing agent. The purchasing agent examines it and also passes upon its propriety, and Upon any suggestions that may be contained as to where the things ought to be bought, or as to prices that should be paid. Starting with the warden's certificate, with the vise of the superintendent, and the vise of the purchasing agent, it comes to the minister, who passes it if he thinks it right and proper. Then it goes back from the minister to the superintendent, and from him to the Purchasing Commission, and the purchasing agent, under the direction of the Purchasing Commission, calls for offers for the supplying of the goods. These offers,

when received, are opened, I think, by the purchasing agent actually in the office of the Purchasing Commission, or, at all events, in the presence of its representative, and the order is awarded to the person who makes the lowest offer. That is the modus operandi.

I do not want to press unduly for information, but I feel with my hon. friend (Mr. Vien), that when the Auditor General's Report is laid before Parliament it should be compared with the Estimates, because it is the foundation of our study of the year's Estimates. I can understand the minister finding some difficulty in answering questions off-hand in regard to the Auditor General's Report, but it does seem to me that if he cannot at this time give the information sought, he should bring it down later and let the item stand until he is prepared to answer questions fully.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend desires that, I have no objection.

I have in my hand a report of last year's operations of the maritime penitentiary situated at Dorchester in my own constituency. I know something about the work done in that institution. As I glance through this report, page after page, my curiosity, at least, if not my suspicion, is aroused, and I cannot help thinking that the minister is not properly advised as to the way in which things are conducted there. The country surrounding that penitentiary at Dorchester, and the city of Moncton adjoining, as well as the city of Sackville, do considerable business in flour and food-stuffs generally, and yet, with few exceptions, in the case of small items which might be called emergency purchases, this report shows only one man in that locality who has supplied anything to the institution during the year. That [DOT] man has a small business concern situated in the parish of Dorchester, and he gets about $17,700 worth of business from the penitentiary. I find that the flour and meat are purchased in Montreal, although a very large proportion of the cattle and meat dealers in Montreal and other cities come right down to my own county, buy beef and take it back to Montreal, when they get the contract to re-ship this meat back to the same locality to feed the convicts in the penitentiary. I do not insinuate that the minister is apprised of the real facts, but it is obvious that there is something wrong somewhere. A dealer in Montreal

cannot possibly sell flour in Dorchester cheaper than a dealer in the Maritime Provinces can, and it does not seem proper that we should get things from outside and pay extra freight, bringing them to the Maritime Provinces from Montreal, Toronto, and elsewhere. Then, I see, Mr. Chairman, if they want a few pounds of clover and grass seed for Dorchester penitentiary a firm in Ottawa furnishes it. I note that 400 pounds of clover seed were purchased in that way; and I suppose at Dorchester they had to wait until word was sent to Ottawa and the purchase made there, although there are at least twenty business houses located not very far from the penitentiary that make a specialty of selling clover and grass seed as my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Elkin) well knows.
Where do they get it?

They get it from the west, and other places. They bring it in and have it on hand, and a telephone order for the articles would bring a response inside of six hours. But no, when they wanted clover seed they had to send to Ottawa for it. It arouses one's curiosity why these things happen. Then too, I notice that when they wanted some cotton duck they sent to New York for it. There were 808 yards of cotton duck bought from a firm in New York for the Dorchester penitentiary. This is but a small matter, but when such things occur year after year it arouses one's curiosity if not one's suspicions; there is a fear that something is working from the inside that the minister does not know about. I would like to have an explanation given why this is so, and why it is that these people at a distance are getting all the business for Maritime Provinces institutions, when the same articles can be obtained in the locality of the institution and at less cost, I believe, than is apparent under this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose my hon.
friend noticed that I was criticized by the gentleman who preceded him because I did not buy everything in the same place.
No, I did not notice it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now I am criticized because I do not distribute the purchases.

My right hon. friend misunderstood me. I was not attempting to argue that. I was arguing that everything should be bought by tender, and I agree with him that contracts should go to the lowest tenderers in all cases, wherever it may be possible; but to me these purchases seem utterly inexplicable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be very glad to take up the items that the hon. gentleman refers to and send him precise information in regard to them. With respect to Mr. Palmer who was mentioned as having supplied goods to the amount of some $17,000, I understand the great bulk of it was coal purchased in the neighbourhood, which is a coal producing country. I have no doubt it will turn out that coal was purchased to the best advantage, and by tender. As regards the purchase of clover seed in Ottawa I would be quite willing to look into it, but I think the hon. gentleman rather conceded himself that if it had been purchased in Moncton the dealer would have been obliged to obtain the clover seed somewhere else.
That may be but there is a dealer there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not any doubt but that the Purchasing Commission got-the colver seed where they could get it to the best advantage. However, I shall be quite happy to look into it and get the necessary information.
The firm in Ottawa would have to purchase the clover seed and resell it; they do not make it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course they do not gather it in the streets of Ottawa. I do not know what the circumstances
10 p.m. were, put perhaps this particular firm in Ottawa were in a better position to handle clover seed at that moment than other firms were. All these purchases were carried out under the system which I explained a little while ago, but as regards any particular transaction, I shall be more than glad to furnish the hon. gentleman with the exact information in connection with the matter.

In view of the fact that the minister is not in a position to-night to give us the exact details of the expenditure during the past year, I purpose dealing with the summary statement as it appears before us for a few minutes. In the first place, I would like to know just how the several totals and increases that appear in the summary statement of the Estimates have been arrived at. I find there is a general summary statement covering the totals for the various penitentiaries. That summary statement covers the amount of $1,371,600 asked for under

this item for the current year. Against that we have a total for the year 1920-21 of $1,096,600, so that this estimate for the current year shows an increase of $275,000 over last year. That is in round figures an increase of twenty-five per cent on the entire estimate. Now, taking the details given in the summary statement under the different headings for the various institutions, we find that' in Kingston the average increase is about twenty-five per cent, and the same with the other institutions all down the line. But when you come to the details you find a wide range of variation. That is the reason that prompts my question as to how these several totals and increases have been arrived at. Is it due to specific reasons in each case or is there a general average for the whole of the Estimates? I find in connection with Kingston penitentiary, under the heading of "salaries and retiring allowances" an increase of $24,500 or an increase over last year of about 19 per cent. I may explain that I have made these calculations hurriedly. I find the salaries and retiring allowance for St. Vincent de Paul augmented by $30,000, or an increase of 35 per cent over last year. I find that the salaries and retiring allowances for Dorchester penitentiary are larger by $23,000, or an increase of 36 per cent over last year. I find that the salaries and retiring allowances for Manitoba penitentiary are larger by $27,000, an increase over last year's Estimates of 66 per cent. In the case of the British Columbia penitentiary the increase for salaries and retiring allowances is only $9,000, or an advance of 17 per cent compared with last year. In the case of Saskatchewan, penitentiary the salaries and allowances are $29,000 more, or an increase of 75 per cent as compared with last year. There seems to be an anomaly here. If increases under this heading are required there should be, I submit- without knowing the reason for these variations, because they have not so far been explained-a general average for the whole service. That is to say that the reasons for an increase with respect to one institution should apply to practically all of the penitentiaries with regard to the same class of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman will find that, subject to particular circumstances in particular institutions- some of which I dealt with this afternoon when I think he was not present-increases attributable to the same causes worked out at a fairly average percentage. Taking

first the increase of $275,000 in the total expense, the sum of $142,500 is required to provide for salaries and retiring gratuities. Of that amount over $100,000 is attributable to increases due to're-classification, $11,000 to promotions of keepers called for under the re-classification, $10,000 to the creation of a school teacher class; and $21,500 to increases in the staff due to increased population, and increases in gratuities resulting from the augmentation of salaries under re-classification. It has been found necessary, also attributable to the increase in our prison population, to make a provision of $24,000 additional for the maintenance of the convicts. That increase in the number of convicts is 391 in twenty-two months, or an increase of twenty-three per cent, and it is estimated that if that rate of increase should continue to March 1922 we would require a further vote. As to the remainder of the additional requirements, there is a sum of $15,000 to complete the work on a new boiler house at the Kingston penitentiary. Some of the boilers there have been in use for over thirty-five years, and we have endeavoured to get the last ounce of usefulness out of them. Now we find it is necessary to replace them and to construct, of course by convict labour, a new boiler house. We have also found it necessary to provide an estimate of $20,000 to cover possible additional cost for coal during the course of the year. Last year our experinece was that we had to pay very much higher prices than we had anticipated.
In Saskatchewan, as I pointed out, there is a much larger increase in the amount asked for than in the case of the other penitentiaries. I explained that, I think, before the hon. member came in. It is attributable to the fact that there we are completing new cell accommodation, which is absolutely necesary because of the increased number of prisoners, mainly due to our making that one penitentiary serve now not only for the province of Saskatchewan but in large measure for the province of Alberta, the balance of Alberta's convicts being provided for in the Manitoba penitentiary. The Alberta penitentiary having been closed this will necessarily work out a very material economy, though at the outset it necessitates some additional expenditures elsewhere. I think I have covered all the observations made by the hon. gentleman.

While the minister has
covered considerable territory, he has failed

to quite grasp my wishes in regard to information. I am sorry that I was not in the House this afternoon when he gave his explanation regarding the increase of $60,000 for land, building and equipment in connection with the Saskatchewan penitentiary. But I find there, as I have already said, increased salary and retiring allowances of $29,000, or an increase over last year of 75 per cent, as against only 19 per cent increase for Kingston and 17 per cent for British Columbia. I find too-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow me to deal with his questions one at a time?
That is what I wanted the minister to do, but he covered the whole field.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me take this one item of the greater percentage of increase of employees at the Saskatchewan penitentiary as compared with similar increases at the penitentiaries. The answer is to be found in what I have already pointed out, that the Saskatchewan penitentiary this year takes over a double burden. We had until the middle of last year an additional penitentiary in Alberta. We have closed that penitentiary and have transferred the bulk of its convicts to the Saskatchewan penitentiary, and of course with this abnormal increase of inmates there necessarily goes an unusual increase of employees to take charge of them. Then, furthermore,-and this applies to all the penitentiaries-we have had to increase the number of employees to meet the very strong representations-and I think justifiable representations-that we ought to make such provision for men tied down to the kind of work that our guards have to do as would enable us to give to each man at least every eighth day off. That would not account for the greater percentage increase in Saskatchewan, but it does account for the increase that runs through the number of employees. Then the classification has added very materially to what we have to pay those employees, and that has involved, as I explained also before the hon. gentleman came in, our making a larger estimate in looking forward to the gratuities that may have to be paid, because their amount is governed by the amount of the salaries paid. The classification also has carried with it the necessity of engaging a larger number of employees owing to the manner in which the duties are now distributed.
I suppose, Mr. Chairman, the classification was inaugurated by the Griffenhagen Company or the Arthur Young Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, we entirely escaped the claws of the Griffenhagen.

The minister evidently believes in Home Rule in penitentiaries as well as in other parts of the world. The next item is maintenance of convicts. I find that whereas in the Kingston penitentiary the maintenance increase is 14 per cent; in St. Vincent de Paul it is 40 per cent; in Dorchester it is 50 per cent, in Manitoba 66 per cent; in British Columbia there is no increase whatever; in Saskatchewan the increase is 66 per cent. I think whoever is in charge of the penitentiary in British Columbia deserves to be well paid for his services, because he is evidently managing that institution along the right lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He manages it so well that he does not get more people coming in there, and that makes a great difference in the percentage increase of cost of maintaining the convicts. That percentage increase in Kingston is very much larger than in the other penitentiaries, but the simple explanation is that the percentage increase of population to be fed, clothed and provided for generally is very much greater in that institution than in the others. If I am not mistaken the percentage increase of population in the Kingston penitentiary is between 60 and 70 per cent; in St. Vincent de Paul I think it is about 48 per cent; and very naturally you have a difference in the percentage increase of cost of maintenance corresponding very accurately I think to the different percentage increase of population. In British Columbia they have no increase of population, and it is natural enough therefore that they should have no percentage increase in the cost of maintenance. Saskatchewan and Manitoba have had to divide between them the penitentiary population that in previous years had been provided for by the Alberta penitentiary, which has been closed; therefore this year they have an unusual percentage increase in expenditure of every kind that attaches to maintenance.

I notice that although
the cost of textiles, fabrics, etc., which would be used in connection with the industries carried on in the penitentiaries, is decreasing, the appropriations under

this head are in most cases considerably increased this year. For Kingston the increase under the head of "industries" is $10,000, or 66 per cent; for St. Vincent de Paul, 50 per cent; for Dorchester, 35 per cent; for Manitoba, 100 per cent. In British Columbia, where there is good management apparently, there is no increase at all. The person in charge there should receive the commendation of the Government; he must be running the institution along the right lines. In view of the fact that materials of all kinds are from 25 to 33J per cent less expensive than last year, I cannot understand why these appropriations should be so much higher. In Saskatchewan the increase is only a slight one, about 8 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The gentleman for
whom my hon. friend has so great an admiration has no increase because he has had no increase in convicts; consequently, he has practically no increase to provide for his industries. The hon. gentleman says there should be a decrease because materials are lower, but the fact is that the bulk of the increase at Kingston, for instance, is for the purchase of machinery.

Would machinery not
cost less for the current year than it did last year?
Mr, DOHERTY: Last year we were not buying any, or very little. We are trying to develop these industries and we have had to procure machinery for that purpose. These are not things which we shall be buying every year, but that expenditure will have to be incurred in Kingston this year. The increase at St. Vincent de Paul under that head of $5,000, is explained by the fact that we are buying less machinery at St. Vincent than at Kingston. At Dorchester the industries are of less consequence and we are investing less in them. At Manitoba also the industries do not play the same important role that they do in the larger penitentiary in the East. We have a smaller provision made in British Columbia; as I say, the industries there are comparatively small. There is nothing in the way of development; therefore we have no additional outlay to make this year. In Saskatchewan the industries play a minor role, though there is an increase of $4,000; some machinery is required there, I believe, for the carpenter shop and the machine shop. But farming is the great industry of the Saskatchewan penitentiary.

I would like, if possible, to get information with regard to the

details of these different items; that is, how much the minister proposes to spend for machinery and farming implements for the different institutions, and how much for textiles, woollen materials, fabrics, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the information with me to-night, but I shall be glad to get it for the hon. gentleman.

We should not pass
these items without knowing how this money is to be spent. I suggest, therefore, that we report progress until such time as we have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, if the hon.
gentleman thinks he requires it, I shall be happy to get it for him, and if he thinks that these items should stand until we can . get this additional information-if he deems that essential to the proper performance of his parliamentary duties-I suppose we shall have to suspend them for the time being. I suggest, then, that we pass to the agricultural items.
We can make progress and deal with those later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen consent to that, I should be glad if the item could be passed; it is the last one I have. Hon. gentlemen may count upon it that I will furnish all this information and, if necessary, make an opportunity for giving it to them. Certainly the opportunity will be forthcoming on the Supplementary Estimates, if not on some other occasion.

Did I understand the
minister to say that the increase in the number of convicts in the Kingston penitentiary is greater than the increase at St. Vincent de Paul?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the increase at
St. Vincent was from 465 to 554, and at Kingston the increase was between 60 and 70 per cent the present population being 721.
Can the minister give us any idea of the cause of the larger increase in Ontario as compared with Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, it would be difficult for me to give the reason. It is fair to Ontario to say that the Kingston penitentiary does get a certain number of convicts who are not chargeable to Ontario- women for instance, and also those convicts who are looked upon as specially incorrigible or dangerous. It is thought that there is better provision in that penitentiary for assuring the detention of ex-

ceptionally violent people, and in that way you must not charge to Ontario all of the surplus population of Kingston penitentiary. Of course, I can appreciate that the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) looks for greater virtue in our province than in the other provinces.

The minister has apparently no idea that the restrictive legislation would have any bearing on the excessive number of convicts over those in other provinces.
. Mr. DOHERTY: I do not know what restrictive legislation the hon. member is dealing wifh. We do not get in the penitentiaries, to any appreciable extent, offenders against prohibitory laws; such offenders go to the jails. The increasing severity of such a law ought not to find itself reflected in an increasing number in the penitentiaries. I do not know that an increased thirst would operate to increase the tendency to crime.
Referring to the Purchasing Commission, we were told by the minister that there were two commissioners, but he did not tell us how many of a staff these commissioners have employed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The staff and so forth of that commission is something entirely outside of my department. I would be glad to get the information, but I do not have it with me. I have not any personal contact with the direction of that department, and consequently, I have not that information.
It appears to apply generally to all the departments of the Government, including the department of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It serves us also, only that I have no connection with its practical operations. It supervises my purchasing as it supervises all the purchasing of the Government; but I am never brought into contact with it, and I never had occasion to inquire how many employees it had. I shall be glad to get the information. The commission reports to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and on some occasion when he is being subjected to the examination of the committee, I have no doubt he would be glad to furnish all details of that kind.

I would suggest that we have the Order in Council under which this commission is appointed.
We have spent a good deal of time discussing this matter, and I should like to know just where we stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to get it.

It has been pointed out to the minister that the authority of the Government to appoint this commission has been challenged by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), who says that the Government has no authority to appoint any commission without a statute. While I have been in the House, I think the practice has been to come to Parliament for statutory authority to appoint commissions. That was the case until the war started, and then the War Measures Act was passed under which a large number of commissions were appointed. The War Measures Act has expired, and the Government has undertaken to appoint a commission without statutory authority, and if it can appoint this commission in that way, I presume it can appoint any commission. The question that makes this matter look a little serious is that on two occasions when the Government came to Parliament for authority to appoint this special commission, opposition developed to the proposal largely on the Government side of the House, and the Government found that it was probably unable to push the matter through. After several attempts to do so, the Bill of last year was withdrawn, and my recollection is that, after it was withdrawn and after Parliament prorogued about the 1st July, in that very same month, the Government, behind closed doors, without authority of Parliament, did the very thing which Parliament refused to give authority to do. The Government appointed a commission by Order in Council, and whether it had authority or not, I submit it was bad practice to do that. I want to ask the minister now, when he comes before the committee again with his Estimates, to produce the Order in Council under which that commission has been appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be glad to see
that the Order in Council is put before the House, but I confess I do not see that it is pertinent to my estimates. I have no desire in the world to avoid the fullest possible discussion of this question of the commission, but I cannot see the usefulness of attaching it to my estimates because that only creates an embarrassment. We have before us no definite question about this commission; we are trying to decide

Would the minister say
that the vote of a sum of money would give impliedly the right to the Government to appoint a commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have always understood that a vote by Parliament of money to be employed by the Government for a specific purpose necessarily involves authority to the Government to do that specific thing. There is another question which the hon. gentleman raised; that is, whether, assuming that we could constitute that commission, we should have gone to the Civil Service Commission to appoint the individuals, I would be happy to discuss all those questions in proper time and place, but I would suggest that, perhaps, the committee might be willing to act upon the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and let this one item, which is the last item I have, pass, with the assurance that upon the Supplementary Esti-

mates, or if I have to make a special occasion, I will give a further opportunity for discussion about the penitentiary purchases; I will procure for the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr.# Pedlow) the information he desires, and if the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) desires special information about the special items he has mentioned, I will furnish it.

I will not insist upon the
details. I only wanted to point out to the minister what occurred to my mind, namely, that a proper system of purchasing should be instituted. The minister told us that the purchases were made through a commission, and naturally we wished to know the character of the commission, information which the minister could not give us. Would the minister be good enough to lay on the Table the Order in Council so that it will be available for the information of the whole House? That would apply not only to the commission created by that Order in Council of 1920, but to all commissions to which the minister has referred to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the Orders in
Council have been laid on the Table on different occasions. I will, however, see that the hon. gentleman gets copies of both.

Is the commission a permanent or a temporary commission? I ask that question because, if it is a permanent commission and the minister is shielding himself behind this commission, we might be more critical of the Estimates than we would be if the minister were prepared to furnish the House with information as to expenditure in his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is nothing permanent in the sense that that commission could not be dispensed with to-morrow if it was thought desirable to do that. There is no fixed period of time-I am speaking from memory, but I feel pretty confident 

for which these gentlemen are appointed. However, we will be better able to discuss that when we have the papers before us.

The minister knows that the appointment of a servant of the state by Order in Council creates what is known as a permanent civil servant, as distinguished from a civil servant temporarily employed under the authority of a minister, and I think if we take the ordinary meaning of the word "permanent" as applied to a civil servant or a commission under the Crown, this is a permanent commission as dis-

tinguished from a commission appointed for a specific purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will find out whether it is or is not a permanent commission, and then we will not have to take time discussing what the meaning of the word is. As I said before, I am not here with the information at my finger tips, but I will see that it is procured.
I wish to ask the minister one more question about the commission?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The chairman has been very lenient to-night, but he must now rule that the constitution of the commission and of previous commissions, while the matter has been allowed to be discussed, is not strictly relevant. The right hon. Minister of Justice has pointed out that fact three or four times, and the chairman must now so rule.

I was just going to ask
whether in future all purchases are to be made through this commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So long as the commission exists, my department will welcome its supervision. We have no desire in the wide world but to have our operations submitted to all possible supervision. As I have already said-I may be blameworthy in that respect, but it never occurred to me that this was a matter to be dealt with in all the fullness of detail incidentally to the penitentiary Estimates-I am not prepared this evening to give the details with regard to this commission, to discuss its constitution, its past, and above all its possible future, but I shall be glad to discuss that question some other time.

This afternoon we voted the salary for a purchasing agent for the Department of Justice. Now if all the purchases are to be made through a commission, I do not see the necessity of having a purchasing agent for the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It may be it is unnecessary, but this is what was thought was wise: although the departments were empowered to do their purchasing, it was thought a wise thing to have the purchasers supervised and to have some co-ordination. I do not say those are the words in which the commission was appointed, but that is the purpose for which it was appointed. We have a number of departments with purchasing agents, and it was thought desirable that you should have some centre that would both see what was going on, supervise what was going on, and give direction
as to how purchases could best be made. It is possible that was not absolutely necessary, but at all events, wisely or unwisely, it was thought to be a useful precaution. But that does not alter the fact that the purchaser retains his functions as purchaser for his particular department. The only difference is that he carries out his work under his general supervision.

I appreciate what the
minister has said as to not being prepared to give detailed information to-night, and in view of that I would suggest that the committee rise and report progress. I should like, however, to ask a question regarding the penitentiary in Alberta. I find that $5,000 is provided for that institution in the Estimates for the current year. I was under the impression that this institution had been closed up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has been closed up, but we still own the property, and there is need for a watchman in charge, and certain other small expenses in connection with taking care of the property. It is a very valuable property, and we hope to dispose of it to very considerable advantage. We are asking this vote of $5,000 so that we may have, something at our disposal to enable us to take care of the property. It may not all be spent.
Has this property been advertised for sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and tenders were called for, but we got no offers that commended themselves to our judgment. I have had the property valued by a gentleman absolutely disinterested, and most highly commended to me, and he puts a very substantial value on the property, but it does not seem to be a fortunate moment to dispose of it. Therefore, we think it is the part of wisdom to hold the property in the meantime and naturally that entails some small expense in taking care of it.

If I read aright the Government's publication there is a substantial reduction in the cost of material and of living generally, but in the Estimates under working expenses and other headings connected with the penitentiaries I find considerable increases. Does not the minister expect that within the coming year there will be a considerable, or at least a certain reduction along these lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We hope for a reduction in the cost of living, but if the cost of living keeps going down and the number
i

of people you have to feed keeps increasing, you cannot expect to feed them on a lesser amount. As to working expenses, if the hon. gentleman had been in the House a little while ago, he would have learned that under this heading are many items that are not affected by the cost of living. For instance, this year, as I explained, we are purchasing in connection with industries a certain quantity of machinery necessary for their operation. These are not things that will be purchased every year, but this year we are seeking to develop our work and have provided for this machinery. But we cannot make comparisons from year to year of expenses of that kind. I had tried to make that clear.
The minister says that he does not expect to have to purchase every year the machinery that he will purchase this year. Does he purchase machinery for all penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Do the working expenses show an increase for all penitentiaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall be glad to
begin all over again and go over the details, but it does seem a little unfortunate that hon. gentlemen should keep on passing in and out while I am giving explanations.
I withdraw the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I try to explain these items as well as I can, but I shall be glad to repeat anything that has not been understood.
Dispense.
Take it as read.
Is the minister sure that the item in the miscellaneous list will be passed by the Minister of Finance? In what way will these items be passed? I refer to page 64.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My past experience
has been that we have never asked for anything under this head-they are only small amounts-which the Minister of Finance or any one else called upon to pass them, has not found to be unreasonable. For example, I do not think it is an unreasonable thing that we should ask for $300 for possible unforeseen expenses in connection with Dorchester penitentiary. I should think that would commend itself as reasonable.

I do not think the minister grasps my point. I find under the general item of miscellaneous in the Estimates there is an item of $80,000 for the Purchasing Commission, I merely wish to know how we are to ascertain which minister will pass these items.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have explained that. As I understand it, the Purchasing Commission reports to the Minister of Finance and-
The Minister of Finance will pass the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I anticipate there will be no difficulty in having the items passed upon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Agriculture-International Institute of Agriculture, ?10,0'00.
What work is done in connection with this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The work carried on by this institute is in connection with the International Bureau of Agriculture which has its headquarters in Rome. All the principal nations in the world are represented, and our branch in Ottawa handles the business for Canada. It handles crop reports received from headquarters. The institute furnishes information concerning supplies of various agricultural products throughout the world, prospects for the future, the growing of crops, probable yields and various statistics of a similar character. We maintain a valuable library in which all this information is gathered for the use of the department or for any one interested.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Live Stock, $1,000,000.
What is the reason for the increase this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The increase is due to increased travelling expenses, additions to some exhibitions that have qualified under the standard for such exhibitions during the past year, to necessary extension work, to the execution of policies already under way, and to general development along these lines. A sum of $25,000 has been set aside to meet probable expansions during the coming year.

The minister spoke the other night about some sires the department lends to different counties. He said that we would deal with this subject when

we reached this item. How many sires are lent altogether to farmers' clubs?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There have been lent to two hundred clubs 2,963 head.

About two months
ago, early in January, a club was formed in Last Mountain constituency and they made application for a sire. That application was turned down in the first instance, the departmental officers expressing the opinion that the club did not need assistance because they were able to buy an animal for themselves. The matter was referred to me and I got into communication with the department, with the result that they reconsidered their decision and agreed to supply an animal. So far, however, that has not been done, at least to my knowledge. The last intimation I had was that the chief of the cattle branch had gone west and hoped to be able to purchase an animal at the spring sales. Two evenings ago, while discussing these Estimates, the member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), informed the committee that some time ago about eighty animals had been supplied to his constituency. Now, the people in my constituency will wonder why it is that it takes them so long to get one animal when eighty can be supplied to some other constituency. Of course, I am aware, that this did not take place during the present minister's regime. Nevertheless, it is the business of his department, and I felt rather keenly the fact that my constituents were not accorded the treatment they deserve. So far as I know, the club at Davidson, Saskatchewan, is the only one in that constituency, and these people are naturally anxious to go ahead. As a matter of fact, they intend building silos and going into the dairy industry in good shape, and I hope the minister will see that their application is honoured and that they are supplied with a sire at an early date.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If this club is qualified, as the hon. member says, there should be no serious delay in supplying it with an animal. Our buyers have been purchasing at the spring sales. One was held at Regina this week, and a number of bulls were purchased, so that my hon. friends constituents will suffer no further delay. However, I shall look into the matter and expedite it as well as I can.
Are these bulls obtained in this country, or are they imported?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
They are bred in Canada and bought at the sales here, and what we
cannot obtain at sales we purchase privately-
Are different breeds supplied?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We supply any breed demanded by a club, but if any club secures an animal for two or three years and then gets another, we do not permit any change in the breed, because we do not encourage cross breeding. We like to keep to certain lines and develop that particular type of animal.
The minister said the other night that these animals were lent for a period of three or four years. At the end of that term, should they not be returned, what action does the department take?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Of course, we see that they are returned at the end of the term. They are usually sold by the agent for beef if they are not fit for further use,, but if they are, they are lent to some other club.
I think the hon. member for Dorchester said last year that some of those lent to his county were not returned.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That was before my
time.
Does the minister know what became of those bulls?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No. I understand this
occurred about four years ago. I cannot give the details as to the disposition of these bulls offhand, but I will be glad to look it up and if the hon. member cares for further information I will be very pleased to give it to him.

I certainly would like
the information, because if the statement of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) is true that eighty head were loaned to the county of Dorchester when the rest of us cannot get any stock for our counties I think we should know what became of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There was no such
number as eighty head loaned to Dorchester county. I never heard of any county getting that number. Altogether, there were only a few bulls, but I cannot offhand give the exact number as the transaction occurred some years ago.

The statement with
which I am credited did not originate from me. I simply repeated what the hon. mem-

ber for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) said the other evening.

Before the item passes
I wish to ask the acting leader of the Government if it is intended to take up any other estimates this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think we will
ask the committee to take up any other estimates after the passage of the few remaining estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would like to finish
the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture. Only two or three items now remain.

Will the minister explain
what he proposes to do with this vote of

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
With pleasure. First
of all we spend money in federal assistance to horse breeding. That is we form stallion clubs throughout the country giving them a certain bonus amounting to about one-third of the cost to assist them in securing animals of high value and in improving the quality of the horse stock of the country. These animals must all pass a careful examination by a veterinarian, must be free from hereditary disease, and be of good weight and good quality. I may say that this is along the line of what is known as the Scotch Premium system for improving horse stock and has been followed with great success in Great Britain.

What amount is to be de [DOT]
voted to that particular purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It will amount to about
$90,000 altogether this year in that particular line.

How long has the system
been in force?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It has been in force
about four years. In addition to that, we have a distribution of pure bred * sires which I described, I think, the other evening. Under this plan in any district where there are no pure- bred sires to be obtained the farmers are permitted to form clubs of ten, and on making proper application to our department we will furnish them with a pure bred sire, loan it to them absolutely free, ship it to the district and pay the freight to the nearest
11 p.m. station. The animals must be maintained by the club and the loan will be for a period of from two to

three years. The benefits particularly derived are these: First, it improves the quality of the cattle in that district; and after five or six years instead of having a number of scrub cattle there we find animals that are pretty well graded up and of fairly good quality. In the second place it is an educational feature of very great value inasmuch as it educates every member of that club to the value of using a pure bred sire. I may say that last year of the cattle inspected and killed in our inspected abattoirs less than ten per cent were fit for export to Europe, showing how necessary it is to raise the quality of our cattle in this country.
What is the amount of that item?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This year the amount is $60,000.
What system of supervision is followed to ensure that the animal is maintained in good condition?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Inspectors visit these
various places and inspect the bulls from time to time. Unless they are maintained in proper condition they are taken away and that club's license is cancelled.
Are the animals returned on demand from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes, they are returned to the department, and, as I pointed out before, are loaned to new clubs or, if their usefulness is over, are sold for beef and the money turned over to the department. In addition to that we have the "Canadian record of performance," which is a system whereby we carry on tests of pure bred dairy cattle throughout the country. For instance, a dairyman has a pure bred dairy herd and he wishes that herd to establish a reputation as a producing herd. On application we send a man to his premises, and he goes through a certain form in entering one, two, three, four, or five cows -whatever number he happens to have at that time. This man instructs the owner in the work to be carried on. The cow's milk is recorded every day. If she is milked twice, it is marked twice; whatever number of times she is milked is recorded. The information is all marked down on a sheet which is kept in the stable in a prominent place. Then our inspector visits the premises regularly from six to eight times a year, takes tests of the butter fat of these herds and carefully inspects the figures regarding the cows, comparing them with the notes he has taken during the

two days he remains on the premises. At the end of the year he is able to tell the amount of the milk yield, and also the amount of butter fat produced by each animal. This system is very valuable indeed in several respects. In the first place it vastly increases the value of that man's herd. I may mention that we have had one cow in British Columbia that produced as high as 33,000 pounds in a year. Similar results, or very nearly as good, have been obtained in other parts of Canada. Such a record gives that cow in that particular locality a special value; not only so, but when the farmer goes into a herd produced from a pure bred sire he is able to look at the record in the pedigree of that animal, and procure a producing animal rather than one which is simply a good looking animal but not descended from producing stock. We are having very great success in connection with this system. Quite a large number of animals have been entered in this record of performance and the number is increasing every year. Up to the present time we have had 15,960 applicants.
What is the amount to be expended for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: $23,880 this year. We likewise have what is known as the car lot policy. I pointed out a moment ago that there are thousands of head of cattle passing through our inspected abattoirs that are unfit to compete in the British market with Argentine or Australian produced beef. The number that is fit amounts to less than ten per cent. These cattle come to our abattoirs in a thin condition, not properly finished and small in size, so that we are doing all that we possibly can to encourage the finishing of livestock in this country. We have therefore introduced what is known as the car lot policy to help to improve cattle along these lines. We will pay the reasonable expenses of a man from the country down to the nearest livestock market and back again, providing he purchases down there one carload of upwards of fifty cattle to take back to his farm.
On what basis is the subsidy given to the man who purchases a car lot of cattle to be finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We simply pay him his
ordinary expenses into the market and out again.

Do you pay the freight
going and coming?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Not unless he takes breeding animals. This is simply his own fare and reasonable hotel expenses.
The item involves an expenditure of how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: About $4,000. Then we have what might be called our rescue policy. During the dry years throughout our western country thousands of young female cattle, sheep and swine that were sent to market either for export to the United States or to be taken by the abattoirs were in such poor condition that when dressed they weighed only from 250 to 350 pounds per head, whereas well-matured animals should dress easily up to 800 pounds. We paid the freight on those animals back to the country points, and in that way since the introduction of that policy we have been able to rescue some 65,000 head of cattle, 60,000 ewes and 350 sows, which are now back on the farms and being used for breeding purposes. Last year on account of two very dry seasons in succession in the southern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan, followed by a very heavy winter which began early in the fall and did not let up until pretty well on in April, if the settlers had been left to their own resources the losses of cattle would have been tremendous. We co-operated with the Provincial Governments and with the railway companies and paid the freight on hay from many other points in Canada for the relief of those cattle. The amount paid out by this department for that particular work was around $500,000. That was one-third of the total, the other two-thirds being contributed by the provincial governments and by the railway companies.
That included freight on the feed?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, just simply to carry out our rescue policy. I understand that in some other departments of the Government it was found necessary to give food to the people themselves.

Was that on the basis of a
loan or a grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A grant. It was simply a case of rescuing those cattle that otherwise would have perished, and many farm- . ers in those sections would have been ruined.
Is it contemplated to continue that help?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No. We have been blessed with one of the best winters we have had

in the West for many years, and cattle are coming in in such good condition that many car loads of good fat grass cattle are going to market three Qr four weeks earlier than last year.
Out of the $975,000 which was expended last year, I understand there was an item of $505,000 for the purpose just mentioned by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, this is an extra item not included in that particular one. It was in the Supplementary Estimates last year.

Have the members of a cattle club any opportunity to make a selection of the bull or bulls which they require? The reason I ask the question is that I have seen several of the Shorthorn bulls put out by the Department of Agriculture, and they are not up to the size they ought to be. As a consequence many of our fat steers are not fit for export, and if we do not have a heavy type of sire, especially for the beef breed, we will not get the heavy export steer.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Nearly all these bulls are yearlings, Mr. Chairman, and unless they are carefully taken care of they will not develop as rapidly as they should. But I think the real cause of the steers not being fit for export, particularly where a pure bred sire is used, is that in many cases the feeding of these animals in their younger years is not carried out as well as it might be. In fact, we all know that in some of the range sections where the grass is pretty well eaten out, the cattlemen depend too much in winter time on a diet of oxygen for their stock and do not give them enough feed.
What were the regulations under which that grant of $500,000 was distributed?

I still maintain that I am quite right in my statement that the bulls which I have seen, especially the Shorthorns, are not of the heavy type. I should add that this was of course before my hon. friend was in charge of the department. I do not care how well you feed the small type, Mr. Chairman, you will never get the weight in the steer that you will if you have the heavy beef type. '

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
These bulls are what
might be called the ordinary field bulls. We do not buy the very highest type of thick low Shorthorn bulls, because they would run into too much money to cross

with scrub cows. However, these Shorthorns are coming down in price now and we will be able to get a very much better quality of animal than we have been able to secure in the past. I admit that some of the bulls sent out by the department have not come up to the handle because with the very high prices prevailing and the keen demand for Shorthorn cattle it was difficult to get the proper type; and, besides, in many cases people demanded the dairy type of Shorthorn.

I understand that the
discretion which the members of a horse club themselves have as to the type of heavy draft horse they will breed, that is, Clydesdale, Percheron, Shire, or others of that nature, does not extend to the lighter grades of horses.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It only extends to the
heavy class of horses because the motor car has had a very serious effect on the light type of horse in this country. For the heavy horse there is always a good market. In some sections of the country there is such a great excess of light horses that we have tried to sell them in Europe in the shape of corned beef in barrels and in boxes, without any great success. I think last year the number of animals of this type which could not be used or sold ran to something like 26,000 head in Alberta, and in British Columbia we have large numbers of light horses and many bands of them running absolutely wild in the valleys. Therefore, on account of the very slight demand for this type we have not encouraged its breeding. Good road horses are still in demand, and also horses that can be used for hunting or saddle purposes.
If a club commences with a Clydesdale horse, does the department demand that the club shall continue the breeding of Clydesdales?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We use our best efforts to have them continue along those lines.

I
should like to get some information from the minister about the clubs that he spoke of as being formed for the purpose of getting stallions for horse breeding. I am not sure that I understood exactly what he said in regard to them. I remember that last year a delegation from my own constituency representing local horse breeders came to Ottawa with the idea of endeavouring to comply with the regulation of the department in order to get one

of the grants mentioned by the minister. 1 understand that some difficulty had been experienced in complying with the regulations on account of the number of farmers who had to sign before anything was done. Is it the case that ten owners of horses are sufficient to form a club?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, there must be ten owners in these clubs, and we assist them by paying one third of the fee.
What I want to know is whether the rules have been modified recently.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, I do not think they have been modified; we have found them acceptable all over the country. I should be very glad to furnish the hon. gentleman with a copy of the rules, and also to meet him and give him any further details he may desire.
If an animal loaned for breeding purposes dies while in possession of the farmers' club, who stands the loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We do. We see, however, that the sire is kept in proper shape. We have travelling inspectors who inspect them from time to time.
And if the animal died from neglect or abuse or lack of proper care, what then?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We stand the loss, and [DOT] in a case of that kind the man responsible would never be furnished with another of these animals. But with our system of inspection we usually get there before the trouble goes so far.
These animals are not insured?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.
Will the minister give me now the information for which I asked?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The amount of freight paid was totalled up and we paid our share, one third, the provincial government and the railways each paying one third.
Who distributed the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Our Live Stock Branch took care of our end of it.
Item 49 does not include any expenditure of the kind referred to by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, it does not include this special relief work.
It seems to me that we are still very far from a million dollars, the amount of this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Oh, I had not finished. In addition to that we carry on a cattle market system, a system of district promoters. All our livestock yards are under propert regulation; we control them in everything they do-in the handling of feed, the fees charged, and so on. We see that the yards are kept in a sanitary condition. In this respect I think we are considerably in advance of our friends to the south of the line. On the 14th of January of this year I attended a meeting held in El Paso, Texas. I attended a similar meeting held there about four years ago, and at that time they were clamouring for such regulations as we now have. When I went down there last year I found they had not even then secured the adoption of such regulations; so we have made good progress along this line. We have a system under which we issue market intelligence from these different yards and furnish market prices that are accepted by the press throughout Canada. The information is sent from one yard to another and to the head office in Ottawa, and we have found that the effect has been beneficial in stabilizing the livestock markets of this country. In addition to that we have promoters out in the country who are encouraging the farmers to sell co-operatively, and the effect has been very marked, particularly in the Maritime Provinces, where the farmers get together and ship co-operatively in carload lots to such markets as Montreal and Toronto, thus securing much better prices than would be received had the animals been sold locally. This has been carried on in connection with our sheep and lamb markets, with very good results. Then, we have assisted in wool grading. We began by grading the wool for our local sheep associations, some of which have now formed a central association with headquarters in Toronto. They handle a large proportion of the wool produced in Canada through a central wool warehouse, and I am glad to learn that they have sold all the wool that has been placed in their hands up to the present time.
What is the nature of the assistance given by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
We began by assisting these associations, doing the wool grading. At first we did it in the field in various sections of the country from the Atlantic
112k,

to the Pacific; now we do most of it in the central warehouse at Toronto. Very much better prices have been obtained through the sale of this wool co-operatively rather than through itinerant dealers.
