In some cases the wool is worth about twice as much as it was at the time it was clipped; in fact we are now getting from 24 to 26 cents as compared with about 15 cents at the beginning of the season.
Is the central warehouse a government property? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, it is rented by this association. What we have been able to do through this wool warehouse compares well with what has been done in the United States. While we have been able to dispose of all our wool, only from 30 to 40 per cent of the pooled wool in the United States has yet been sold. Another thing has been gained as a result of our grading; we find that our Canadian manufacturers are using more Canadian wool this year than they ever did before, and the wool owners, hearing about the success of this co-operative associations, have started the movement of their wool through the cooperative warehouse.
How much is the Government spending for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
On the wool grading service this year, about $8,000. In connection with the handling of eggs, we have formed egg circles throughout the country, through which last year we were able to sell 300,000 dozen eggs out of a total export of 600,000 dozen. This system is carried out in a big way in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Ontario. The farmers agree to market cooperatively through a collector. These egg circles join other egg circles, secure a paid salesman and market to the best of their ability, thus securing very much better prices by keeping their eggs in proper condition. Under the old system they took their eggs into the country store and traded them for groceries, and as the eggs were often retained there for much longer period than they should have been, the city consumer was not always satisfied when the product finally reached his table.
We have had developments along similar lines in connection with dressed poultry. We are also carrying on a system of market reports in connection with the egg business, so that producers are continually informed as to egg market prices and are thus always able to get the best prices. We also carry on egg inspection for interprovincial

movement and export; that is, eggs passing from one province to another and eggs that are exported to Great Britain. We are also carrying on now a record of performance for poultry. That is something that was not thought of in past years. We have set two standards-the hen that will lay 150 eggs in a year or a flock that will average 150 eggs per bird for a general record, and then the accredited hen with a high record of 225 eggs per year. The owners of hens producing those numbers of eggs are given a certificate to that effect, and cockerels or young roosters are registered when they come from dams possessing such records. In that way we produce a high standard of poultry, and by careful selection and breeding we have been able to bring the production of a single hen all the way from an average of 65 to 300 eggs in a year. Let me give an illustration to show what that is worth. If the produce of the 40,000,000 hens in Canada to-day could be increased by only one dozen eggs per hen in a year, that would amount to nearly $13,000,000 a year, so that it can be seen that there is an immense field ahead of us in increasing the production of our poultry.
What is the nature of your service and assistance in that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: As regards the improvement of the eggs, the work is carried on at our experimental farms, and as regards the hen registration, the records are taken by representatives of our Poultry Branch which is connected with the livestock Department.
Is there any grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, but there are wages, travelling expenses and so forth to pay in that connection.
For the officials?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In connection with the livestock service, we control the export under the Livestock and Livestock Products Act. The operations of stock yard management and the fees are controlled by our department. The operations of members of commission firms are under our department. The commission men are bonded, so that in the event of a commission man making a sale of cattle and getting away with the funds, we can recover. We carry on a bying service for farmers. Our representatives are always at the yards, and if a man is inexperienced in taking over a lot of cattle, he can go to one of our men who will give his assistance and start him on his way, and also give him information how to ship to the best advantage.

As regards the-bonding of these commissioned men, I understand a little while ago there was a serious failure in connection with one of these firms in Winnipeg. How is the amount of the bond established? Is there a sliding scale, or is the bond just a fixed one?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is no sliding
scale; the fixed sum is $10,000. We have been carrying on a system of exhibits at exhibitions. Many hon. members who have visited our big exhibitions have, no doubt, seen our exhibits of wool and eggs, candling eggs, and also some very temping looking samples of lamb and pork which were made of plaster of Paris and properly painted so that they made a very good imitation of the real article, the idea being to show the people the particular types demanded by the market and the most profitable ones to produce.
We have given grants to our summer fairs, and this year we have set aside a sum of $98,000 while the sum set aside for grants to winter fairs amounts to $25,000. We add prorata to the amount given by the fair in prizes up to $5,000. If a fair will give $2,500 in prizes, we add dollar for dollar to that. These winter fairs are fat stock shows, and this assistance is given with a view to encouraging the finishing, of our cattle.
Do you give these grants to all country fairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No, only to those that
can qualify under the cash system.

What is the minimum in
prizes that the local fair has to put up?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: A summer fair must pay at least $4,000 of its own money for livestock before receiving assistance.
Are those grants limited to livestock?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Livestock and poultry.
We figure that the smaller country fairs come within the purview of the Provincial Government. We are giving our assistance to the big exhibitions. We are giving $25,000 a year to the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair Association of Toronto. This is a new exhibition established there along the lines of the big international show in Chicago. The big show in Chicago is one that has rendered a very valuable service to the livestock interests on both sides of the line, and on some occasions our Canadian breeders have been able to go over and compete with American breeders and win out. Anyone visiting that show would
be astounded at the size of it and the high quality of the cattle exhibited there.

May I point out to the minister the advisability of the department assisting these county fairs, not only the livestock or poultry ones, but all country fairs? As I pointed out when discussing the item of experimental farms the other night, very few methods of assisting agriculture generally are more progressive and practical than these county fairs which permit farmers to get together in the principal place in the county and see what has been done by the best and most progressive farmers of the districts. These county affairs are assisted by the Provincial Governments, but I think the Federal Government should also give assistance along that line. Last year, for instance, I tried to obtain a grant for the county fair of Lotbiniere, which is one of the finest county fairs in my section of the province and which has been commended by the local Minister of Agriculture for its progressive methods. I would like the Department of Agriculture to take these county fairs into consideration and to see whether they could not divert some of the money or ask a vote from Parliament for assisting these county fairs in their local exhibitions.

I should like to endorse
the suggestion of my hon. friend from Lotbiniere, not only as regards his county, but also the county of Kamouraska, of which I have spoken twice already during the discussion of the Estimates of this department. At St. Pascal, the county seat of Kamouraska, we not only hold a county fair each year, but we have there a large, splendid permanent building, built especially for exhibiting cattle. The father of my hon. friend from South Quebec (Mr. Power), who died last fall, had a farm in the county of Kamouraska and he was in the habit of exhibiting a great many thoroughbred cattle In this building at the county seat. I think in view of all the efforts that have been made in the past by the people of the county of Kamouraska for the development of agriculture, they should certainly receive some share of the money that is allotted by the department for these fairs.

Notwithstanding what
has been said by my hon. friend from Lotbiniere and my hon. friend from Kamouraska, their county fairs are not to be compared with the county fair we have in L'Islet.

I take strong objection to
that statement.

Kamouraska is the only
county that has a permanent fair building.

If I can persuade the
minister to make a grant towards the fair in our county, I shall be very glad.

Those of us who are interested in a practical way in agriculture have heard with pleasure the description that has been given by the minister of the activities of the Livestock Branch in the marketing of livestock and livestock products. I think we in Eastern Canada have probably come closer to the officials and have had a better opportunity of seeing how the money was expended among the farmers to encourage co-operative marketing than have other parts of Canada, and I want particularly to say that a great deal of benefit has been derived during the past few years, and especially during the past season, through the assistance of the department's representatives in the marketing of livestock. There is one thing that the farmers in our co-operative associations are not very expert in, and that is in securing proper means of transportation over long distances. In that respect we have received a great deal of benefit during the past year from the livestock representative stationed at Moncton. We have also received a great deal of benefit in a general way from the Poultry Branch. I find on looking over the Estimates that the minister has brought down that the appropriation for the general conduct of the department this year is smaller than last year by about $250,000. The large item of $390,000 for the Health of Animals Branch represent an increase, but there have been decreases in the other items. I hope it is not the intention of the minister in any way to decrease the staff in the marketing or Livestock Branch, who are assisting the farmers in the marketing of livestock, hogs, sheep, poultry and eggs. It is important from the standpoint of the agriculturists of Eastern Canada that the expenditure on that work be increased. If we do not keep pace with the times and follow up the work that has already been done, we are apt to lose the benefit of what has already been accomplished. Speaking from personal knowledge of conditions in Eastern Canada, I think this Parliament and the people of this country generally would endorse the expenditure of more money in giving assistance to farmers' associations that have organized themselves in a co-operative way to reach the larger markets of Canada. As is well known to the members of this House, in marketing 
our livestock it is necessary for the farmers in Eastern Canada to ship to the city of Montreal, where the nearest stockyard and abattoir are located. We have norte closer to take care of the surplus stock for which there is not a market in Eastern Canada, and it is necessary that the assistance that has been given during the past year be increased next season. If I judge correctly the sentiment of our people, and the progressive spirit they are showing in co-operating with the agents of the department in marketing their livestock, I am sure that a larger number of stock will be shipped to the stockyards of Montreal and Toronto next year than during the past year. I would particularly urge upon the minister to persuade, if possible, his associates in the Government to allow him a little more money than he has asked for in his Estimates for the development and carrying on the work of the Livestock Branch.

I wish to say a word in reference to the bonding of livestock. commission men on the stock yards. The minister said that they were bonded so as to safeguard the stockmen who ship their stock to the yards against loss and so that they would be sure of receiving their money, but that is not always the result. Reference has already been made by the hon. member for Battleford to the failure of a firm in Winnipeg last fall. I have been informed that several stockmen lost heavily on shipments of stock through the failure of that firm. I think a bond of about $10,000 is not sufficient; the amount ought to be very considerably increased.
I also wish to say a word or two in regard to the work of some of the officials of the Live Stock Branch, and particularly in regard to the work being done by the official stationed in the city of Winnipeg. Mr. Johnson is doing excellent work there in educating the farmers to ship on the co-operative plan. The farmers will accompany a carload of steers to the stock yards, and in that way they see just what a fat steer ought to look like, and learn to judge just when their cattle are fit to ship. Then there is this further advantage, that they can ship back again a carload of steers for stockers. I wish to congratulate the minister upon carrying on this work and I [DOT]'hope he will see that it is continued. I would also impress upon him the importance of giving careful attention to the bonding of the livestock commission merchants.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That question is under consideration at the present time.

I should like to endorse what my hon. friend from Queen's P.E.I. (Mr. Sinclair) has said as to the assistance the farmers have received from the officials of the department in the shipping of their livestock. I have been chiding my hon. friend since he sat down for not going far enough. As he has said, we have to ship our_ stock to Montreal because we have no nearer market in the Maritime Provinces for our livestock. The other evening the minister said that an abattoir and cold storage plant had not been built in the Maritime Provinces because there was not enough stock in sight to keep it running the year around or make it profitable. Personally I think there never will be unless the abattoir and cold storage are started first. The plant could be started on a small scale, and once started, I am sure that business would increase very rapidly. At the present time our livestock must be shipped to Montreal or some other point in order to get the facilities of the abattoir and cold storage plant. Then the meat products have to be shipped back to us in Eastern Canada and we are therefore in the position of having to pay freight both ways. We pay freight on the livestock to the abattoir, and our dealers pay freight on the meat going back again to the eastern provinces. In the eastern provinces our winters are long and severe. Most of our farmers who have any stock to sell have to dispose of it at a time of year, towards the fall, when cattle are not easily fattened in the warm weather, principally by grazing. At that time there are no facilities for handling stock to be sold in the Maritime Provinces and the farmer gets a small price for his cattle. Unfortunately, we do not do enough winter feeding. If we had enough fat stock for sale at the time of year, round about Easter, when high prices obtain, and if we had facilities for handling cattle in the Maritime Provinces, the stock industry would develop very rapidly. We have a good country for growing stock, but we lack facilities to enable us to take advantage of the opportunities that offer. With regard to the grants to agriculture, I was interested to hear the minister's statement on this subject. Has any grant been applied for by the agricultural society with headquarters in Woodstock, Carleton county, New Brunswick? If so, what prospect is there of this grant being given?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No formal application
has been made. Judging from the report for last year, they have apparently qualified for the grant this year.

I should think so. I heard hon. members boasting about the exhibitions they have; they claim they have the best buildings and grounds for exhibitions. I would invite, not only the Minister of Agriculture, but those members who have been bragging about their facilities for holding exhibitions, to go to Woodstock, New Brunswick, and see one of the most beautiful spots on earth for an exhibition.
We shall be delighted.

It is on an angle of
the St. John river, reached by a bridge. I do not know the exact amount expended by that society in the past two years, but I know that they have spent something like $80,000 for buildings and a race course. People from the United States go to the exhibitions there and they tell us that the ground at Woodstock is the most beautiful they have ever visited. I hope, therefore, the minister will see his way to give us a substantial grant to assist our society.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Seed and Feed Control, $240,000.

Will the minister give us
some explanation of this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In connection with the
seed department, during the winter and fall months we carry on a system of inspection of seeds. These seeds are carefully examined at our different laboratories which are established in various parts of the country, the object being to secure a supply of pure seed to the farmers. In summer, we encourage the growing of good seed in communities, and aim at having them grow particular kinds of seed, so that purchasers may buy in carload lots. We also establish seed fairs, and have field men demonstrate the necessity for the use of good seed and how best to produce it. Our experimental farms carry on experiments with new varieties, or with varieties they have already produced. When these are found to be of substantial value, they are taken out by the seed branch and further developed along commercial lines in centres where we attempt to get as many good first class farmers as possible interested in the production of A1 seed. This is of the very greatest possible importance to agriculture in Canada. Poor seed is like poor stock; you cannot expect good results from poor seed

any more than you can expect good results from a scrub bull. So that, excellent results have been obtained. We also have a system of producing what is known as pedigreed seed. A pure strain is secured and developed, and after a careful selection running over a period of three years, when the varieties reach that state of purity that satisfies the inspector, after they have gone through the full process, they are accepted' as pedigreed seed.

Does this item comprise
grants of seed, or grants of money as prizes for first class grain?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The sum of $60,000 is
granted to seed fairs, and in the marketing of seeds there is an organization in the local seed centre, and interprovincial and export trade is developed. Through the action of this particular branch we have been able to secure our own root seeds. We have greatly increased the production of timothy and other grass and clover seeds. Many of these seeds before the war were entirely imported. We carry on a publicity campaign with a view to directing attention to the value of Canadian grown seed, and we have also done a certain amount of work in connection with development of fibre flax and the inspection of potatoes. We have inspected during the last year, in the St. Lawrence valley, 171 car loads of seed potatoes. We also carry on seed grading at the terminal elevators. Seed is graded according to standard for home use and export. This particular branch carried on what was known as the Seed Purchasing Commission during the war with a view to securing a supply of pure seed so as to encourage greater production, and they were able since 1916 to do a business amounting to nearly $16,000,000 of clean and graded seed. The seed is forwarded to any person in Canada on application, and is shipped on sight draft. After expending all this money, I am glad to be able to say that they were in a position to get returns for every dollar, to pay all expenses and a fair rate of interest on the money. This particular branch controls ordinary feeds, such as bran, shorts, etc., under the new Act passed last year. Our men receive complaints from time to time regarding the condition of these feeds, and they make investigations to see that the law is complied with. But in view of the fact that the law has been in operation only a short time, our work so far has consisted largely in a campaign of education. Our men go
tMr. Tolmie.]
into the various mills where feeds are mixed and take samples of them before they go into the hopper in order to secure information showing the value of the seed and as to whether the producer or manufacturer is complying with the law as to the ingredients he uses in various feeds. That is the general line of the work which is being carried on by this branch, which we consider one of the most important in the Department of Agriculture.
Will the Seed Commission be continued in existence this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, it will.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant to National Dairy Council, $3,000.
What is the National Dairy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This Council is composed of representatives from all the dairy associations in the various provinces of Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On the motion of the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty the House ajourned at 11.55 p.m.
Monday, March 21, 1921.
